conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had nausea and vomiting again, and bad belly pain. I’ve been doing that G-tube venting like before, and it helped a little, but then I started vomiting again even after venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before with partial bowel obstructions. Did you pass any stool or gas recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a solid bowel movement with a Fleet enema yesterday—started solid, got a bit loose—but no gas. I’m still not feeling right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from today. It shows your small bowel is dilated, and there’s contrast in the large bowel, which suggests a partial blockage or ileus, similar to what you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not completely blocked? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s partial, which means things are still moving, just slowly. We’ll manage this without surgery for now. You’ll be on nothing by mouth—NPO—for a few days, and your G-tube will be left open to gravity to help drain fluid and reduce pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being on NPO. But I guess it’s necessary. What about pain? It’s pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV morphine every six hours, starting at 6 mg. We’ll adjust it based on your pain. But we have to be careful—too many narcotics can slow your bowels even more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ve been on MS Contin at home. Can we keep that going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your MS Contin 30 mg twice daily. We’ll also keep your pregabalin for nerve pain. And for nausea, we’re using Phenergan since you’re allergic to Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really can’t take Zofran—it doesn’t help anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll stick with Phenergan. Your labs show your hemoglobin is low—11.2—so we think you have iron deficiency anemia, likely from malabsorption. We’ll give you IV iron—Ferrlecit—tomorrow to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve always had trouble absorbing nutrients. What about my Coumadin? I’m on it for my arm clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your warfarin at 7.5 mg daily. Your INR is therapeutic, so we’re good there. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but maybe a little less pain. My G-tube drained over 1200 cc yesterday. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected with a partial obstruction. The good news is your output is a sign the tube is working. We’re seeing it trend down today—already under 1000 cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any chance I can start drinking something soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to see your bowels start moving more normally. You’re still having some distension and tenderness. We’ll repeat the CT if things don’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Your G-tube output is now down to about 600 cc. That’s a great sign. You passed a bowel movement with Miralax yesterday—your lower pain improved after that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the lower pain is gone. The upper belly pain is still there, but less sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team suggested gentle abdominal massage to help move things along. It might help relieve the remaining blockage. Would you be okay trying that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sure, I’ll try anything. Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t. We’ll do it gently. The idea is to stimulate motion past the sluggish part of your bowel. You might pass gas or feel some cramping—that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job. After the massage, you passed gas, and your G-tube output increased. That means things are moving. Your pain has improved too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I feel like a weight lifted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we wanted. We’re starting you on peripheral TPN today—total parenteral nutrition—because you’ve been NPO for three days. It’ll give you calories and nutrients through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPN? I’ve had that before. It’s okay, but I’d rather eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But we need to be sure your bowel is ready. We’ll try a full liquid diet tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without nausea or vomiting. We’re going to try a full liquid diet today—broth, juice, pudding. We’ll start slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’m so happy! Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll monitor you closely. If you tolerate it, we’ll keep you on liquids and clamp your G-tube to see if it stays down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The TPN is infusing now. You’re doing well on liquids so far. No vomiting, and your belly is softer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel good. Just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal after a few days of fasting. We’re also adjusting your pain meds. We’re stopping the IV morphine and switching you to oral MS Contin 30 mg three times a day. Less IV narcotics help your bowels recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll take the pills. Can I still have liquid morphine if it flares up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2.5 ml every four hours as needed. But we’ll watch for sedation. Your pregabalin dose is also adjusted—75 mg in the morning and at bedtime, plus one at noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days on liquids with no vomiting. Your G-tube has been clamped, and you’re not having pain. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on full liquids for one week. Take Miralax once a day to keep your bowels moving. Continue your regular meds—misoprostol for your stomach, pilocarpine for dry eyes, and warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with MS Contin 30 mg every 12 hours for five days, then taper. Use liquid morphine for breakthrough pain. Call us if you have severe pain, fever, or can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—see your primary doctor and Dr. ___ in one month. We’ll also check your INR and iron levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: full liquids for a week, Miralax daily, and your meds. Walk every day to keep things moving. Call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m so grateful for the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in this morning with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. Yesterday afternoon I tried eating a sandwich—my first solid food in a while. About two hours later, I started vomiting everything—food, liquids, even my pills. I estimated maybe 3000 cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had this before with partial bowel obstructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like my past episodes. I put my G-tube on suction right away, but not much came out. I’ve also had diarrhea—watery at first, now small pellet-like stools. No blood though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER, they did an X-ray and removed about 1500 cc from your G-tube. Your CT scan this morning shows early signs of a partial small bowel obstruction, likely triggered by advancing to solids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a full blockage? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not complete. There’s dilation in the small bowel, but air and stool are still moving into the large bowel. That’s good. We’ll manage this without surgery—NPO for now, IV fluids, and keep your G-tube on suction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not worse. But I was hoping I could finally eat solids again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your body needs time. We’ll start with clear liquids once your nausea improves. GI is consulting today to help guide the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diarrhea—should I restart Miralax?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped it for now. The diarrhea may be from the obstruction or rapid transit. We’ll monitor. Stool tests came back negative for infection, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your G-tube output has decreased from 1500 cc to about 600 cc since being NPO. That’s a good sign the bowel is calming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. My nausea is better too, especially with the Phenergan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping that on board. Your labs show mild dehydration and low hemoglobin, but stable. No signs of infection. We’ll continue IV fluids and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fibrosing mesenteritis making this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s part of the picture. The CT shows chronic changes and a possible remnant GJ tube in the bowel that could be a focus for inflammation. That may contribute to these intermittent blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that tube—it was removed years ago. I didn’t know it could still cause issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon. For now, we focus on conservative management. Tomorrow, if you’re stable, we’ll try advancing to full liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without suction on the G-tube and no vomiting. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with small sips of water, then advance to full liquids—broth, juice, pudding. We’ll watch closely for nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’m still on morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added sustained-release morphine twice daily and liquid for breakthrough pain. We’ll keep that on discharge since your pain has improved but may linger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the liquid diet well—no vomiting, good bowel sounds. GI agrees we can keep progressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you continue doing well, possibly tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re stable without G-tube suction and on a full liquid diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I take it for my DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued it at a slightly higher dose—7.5 mg daily. Your INR was in range yesterday, so that’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my dry eyes and mouth—should I keep using the drops and pilocarpine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Those help with your Sjogren’s. We’ve kept all your regular meds except adjusting timing for hospital routines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve gone over 24 hours without G-tube suction and no issues. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What should I eat when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on full liquids for the next few days—smoothies, soups, yogurt. If you’re doing well, you can slowly try soft solids, but stop if nausea or pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube? Should I keep it on suction at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you start vomiting or feel bloated. Otherwise, keep it clamped. Use it for meds if needed, but crush and dissolve them well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about warning signs? When should I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, severe pain, persistent vomiting, or blood in stool, go to the ER. Otherwise, follow up with your GI doctor in a week to discuss advancing your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds—how long should I take the morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it as prescribed for now. As your bowel function improves, you’ll likely need less. Your doctor can adjust it at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better and more confident going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you in good condition. Keep up with fluids, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Rest at home and we’ll see how you progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will go over your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready whenever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get everything set up. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take care until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep monitoring how you feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling much more hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Recovery takes time, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take it easy and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this admission. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having sharp pain in my upper abdomen, constant nausea, and dizziness when I stand. I threw up once—greenish, not bloody. I haven’t eaten much—just a little pudding yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds similar to your past episodes. You’ve had several hospitalizations recently for partial bowel obstructions, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, five in the last three months. I was just discharged two days ago on a full liquid diet, but the pain and nausea came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We reviewed your CT scan from today. It shows no major change from the one five days ago. There’s still a piece of old tubing in your small bowel that might be causing irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tubing from my old GJ tube? I thought that might be the issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The scan shows new wall thickening around that area, which could be contributing to the partial obstruction. But there’s no sign of a complete blockage or free air, so surgery isn’t needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan? I’m so tired of being sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue with bowel rest—no food by mouth for now. You’ll get fluids through an IV, and we’ll manage your nausea with Phenergan and your pain with your usual morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube? It’s been draining a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep it to gravity drainage, not suction. It’s helping decompress your stomach. Also, we’ve scheduled to replace the G-tube tomorrow—it was already planned, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been leaking a bit. I’m glad we’re doing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The procedure is low-risk and will be done under fluoroscopy to make sure the new tube is placed correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but the pain is a little less. I’m really weak and dizzy when I try to sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low this morning—75 over 51 when you stood. That explains the dizziness. We’re giving you more IV fluids to help with dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been dizzy for months, but it’s worse now. Is that from the bowel issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Dehydration and not eating are making it worse. We’ll keep monitoring it. Your labs show your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR? I’m on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PTT was high on admission—150—but it’s coming down. We’ll check it again soon. No bleeding, so we’re continuing your warfarin at the same dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you for your G-tube replacement. Any questions before we go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? How long does it take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation, so you’ll be relaxed. It usually takes about 30 minutes. They’ll confirm the placement with contrast to make sure it’s in the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went perfectly. The new G-tube is in place, and the contrast confirmed it’s in the stomach. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a little pressure, but no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep it clamped for a bit, then start with gravity drainage. Once you’re stable, we’ll try advancing your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea has improved, and the G-tube output has decreased. We’re going to try starting you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have some broth or apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with small amounts. We’ll also clamp the G-tube for 45 minutes after each intake to see how you tolerate it without drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the liquids. No vomiting, and the clamp test was successful. We’re going to advance to full liquids—like yogurt, pudding, and Ensure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’m hungry. But I’m worried about the Ensure—won’t that affect my phosphate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your phosphate was high this morning—6.3. You’ll need to take two TUMS with each bottle of Ensure to bind the phosphate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is normal, no infection. Liver and kidney function are stable. We’ll check your INR and phosphate again before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on full liquids for over 24 hours with no issues. The G-tube has been clamped, and you’re not needing suction. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well today, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll stay on full liquids and follow up with your GI doctor before trying solids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? Are they changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No major changes. We’re increasing your trazodone to 150 mg at bedtime for sleep. Everything else stays the same, including your warfarin and thyroid meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Phenergan for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll keep that as needed, especially before meals. We’re sending home 120 tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest INR is 2.8—perfect for warfarin. Phosphate is 5.9, so still a bit high. Keep taking TUMS with Ensure and limit to three bottles a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. When do I get the lab work done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have blood drawn three days after discharge to check INR and phosphate. Call your primary doctor with the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Vital signs are stable, pain is controlled, and you’ve tolerated full liquids without nausea. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER if you have fever, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or shortness of breath. Otherwise, keep on full liquids and follow up with GI in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube site? Any signs of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it clean and dry. If it becomes red, swollen, or starts draining pus, let us know. Right now, it looks clean and healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired but much better. Ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember: full liquids, TUMS with Ensure, no solids yet, and follow up with GI. We’ll send your discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your prescriptions and instructions. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take it slow at home and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’ve reviewed the discharge instructions and have all your meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s here. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re cleared to go home. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your dizziness has improved, but be careful when standing. Rise slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been doing that the last few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep up the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here to take you home. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. All set to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all set. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting this morning after taking your medications and Boost. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. I’ve had this kind of pain before, but this episode was worse. I vomited about 1000cc of greenish fluid, and the pain didn’t go away completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis was just reviewed. It shows no new obstruction or acute issue. The loops of small bowel look unchanged from your prior scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a blockage? But the pain feels similar to when I’ve had partial obstructions before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s likely related to your fibrosing mesenteritis and chronic GI dysmotility. There’s no surgical obstruction, but your bowel isn’t moving things through well, which can cause pain and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t passed gas since yesterday, but I did have a formed bowel movement the day before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your G-tube output is stable. We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now—no food by mouth—and give IV fluids to rehydrate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been dizzy when standing, like last time. Is that still related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely due to dehydration from vomiting. We’re giving fluids, and that should help. Your blood pressure was low in the ER—96/64 now—and heart rate was high at 112, which fits with volume loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my Coumadin? I’m on warfarin for DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your INR. It was elevated at 3.5, so we held your warfarin dose today. We’ll restart it tomorrow at a lower dose once it comes down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I don’t want to bleed, but I also don’t want a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Your INR should normalize soon. We’ll continue your home dose once it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your white blood cell count was high—14.1—but that’s likely from dehydration, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired? I didn’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, dehydration can cause fatigue and elevate WBC. Your count is already coming down with fluids. Also, your kidney function was affected—creatinine was 1.4, up from your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. Is it permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s likely prerenal—meaning due to low blood flow from dehydration. Your creatinine is already improving to 1.0 with IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the urine test? I saw it was cloudy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture showed mixed bacteria, but it’s consistent with skin contamination—likely from how the sample was collected. No UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection anywhere. Your chest X-ray shows a small area at the left base—could be atelectasis or early pneumonia—but you’re not coughing or short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel fine breathing. Should we treat it just in case?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch it. If you develop fever or cough, we’ll reconsider. For now, focus is on hydration and bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start advancing your diet slowly. You can try clear liquids now—water, broth, apple juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to eat something. Should I clamp the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll clamp it while you’re on oral intake. We’ll monitor for nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight—no nausea. We’re upgrading to full liquids: Ensure, pudding, yogurt. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some discomfort around the G-tube site, but not sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’re continuing metoclopramide and misoprostol to help with motility. We increased misoprostol to 200mcg four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the increase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To improve gut motility. Given your history of recurrent SBO and gastroparesis, stronger stimulation may help prevent future episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as directed. What about the pregabalin change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll now take an extra 75mg dose at noon and 5 PM, in addition to your usual twice-daily dose. It may help with nerve-related pain and overall discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using morphine, but I’d like to rely on it less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re transitioning you back to your home pain meds. You can use the liquid morphine as needed, and the sustained-release tablet twice daily for baseline control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on full liquids for a day and tolerated them well. We’re adding soft solids—cottage cheese, mashed potatoes. How’s nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only mild nausea this morning, gone after taking Phenergan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your hemoglobin was high on admission—41.3—but that was from hemoconcentration. It’s now down to 32, which is your baseline, so no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about anemia. But I’ve had chronic anemia for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely anemia of chronic disease. We’re not changing anything—just continuing to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8, which is in range. We’ve restarted your warfarin at 2.5mg daily—three pills of the 2.5mg strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take that in the morning with my other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well—ambulating, eating soft foods, pain controlled. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need IV fluids at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can use normal saline—500cc boluses if you feel dehydrated, nauseated, or have pain. Or continuous at 100cc/hr if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used that before. It helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up with home care. Also, keep taking misoprostol and the new pregabalin schedule. Follow up with GI soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow morning. You’re tolerating food, pain is controlled, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll watch for fever or severe pain and go to the ER if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. No nausea today, and I walked the hallway twice yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Continue full liquids and soft solids. Use IV fluids as needed. Call your doctor if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll schedule the GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You’re here because of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A few days ago, I started feeling nauseous again. Yesterday it got worse—I couldn’t keep anything down, and I felt dizzy just standing up. I’ve barely peed in over a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your G-tube has been draining more than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, more output than normal. I called my doctor and tried Gatorade, but it didn’t help. I knew I might need fluids again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’ve started IV fluids, and you’ll stay NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But the pain is bad. Can I get something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV Dilaudid for pain and Phenergan for nausea. But we have to be careful—pain meds can sometimes make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s happened before. I take morphine at home, but it makes me sicker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s part of the cycle we’re trying to break. We’ll monitor your response and adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your X-ray came back. No sign of a bowel obstruction. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It looks like your usual ileus—your gut isn’t moving well due to your fibrosing mesenteritis. We’ll keep supporting you until it recovers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. It feels like my other flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We checked your labs. Your kidney function is a little off—creatinine is 1.1—but that’s likely from dehydration. The fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not long-term. It’s called prerenal kidney injury—your kidneys are stressed from low volume, but they’ll bounce back with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your blood pressure dropped a bit this morning—systolic in the 70s. You felt dizzy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little lightheaded when I sat up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s from the pain medication. We held the IV narcotics for now and increased fluids. You’re stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the morphine might have caused that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It can lower blood pressure, especially when you’re dehydrated. We’ll switch back to your oral meds when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chronic pain team reviewed your case. They recommend using IV Toradol in the future instead of narcotics during flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s Toradol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a non-opioid pain medicine. It works well for abdominal pain and doesn’t worsen nausea like opioids can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. I’d rather not feel sicker from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Agreed. We’ll note that for future admissions. They also suggest Lidoderm patches if your pain is localized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped from 12.3 to 9.8. But we checked for bleeding and hemolysis—nothing there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I anemic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a dilutional anemia—your blood got diluted from all the IV fluids. Your counts should normalize as things balance out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. Your body is adjusting. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR came back at 2.3—perfect. We’ll keep you on your usual warfarin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had clots before, so I don’t want to mess with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re continuing your levothyroxine too—thyroid levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable for hours. We’re going to try advancing your diet—start with ice chips and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous—last time I tried, I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. We’ll give anti-nausea meds ahead of time and watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’ve tolerated liquids and soft foods. Your pain is controlled on your oral morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re discharging you today. We’re increasing your misoprostol to 200 mcg four times a day to help gut motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That was adjusted last time too. I’ll keep track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, continue your home pregabalin and metoclopramide as needed. And follow up with your pain clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another hospital stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. But if symptoms return, try oral rehydration first. If you can’t keep fluids down or feel weak, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more CT scans unless it’s an emergency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. The team agrees—your history and X-rays are enough. We’ll avoid unnecessary radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much more confident about managing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all instructions to your primary team. Rest well, and don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re here because of abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain has been coming back like it has before—crampy, all over my belly. I’ve been nauseous and threw up a couple times. I also feel really dehydrated—my mouth is dry and my urine is dark.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We saw in your imaging that there’s no bowel obstruction, but your colon is quite full of stool. This could be contributing to the discomfort. We also hooked your G-tube to gravity drainage to help relieve pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds familiar. I’ve had this before with my fibrosing mesenteritis. Is that what’s going on again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like a flare of your fibrosing mesenteritis. We’re giving you IV fluids for dehydration and medications for pain and nausea. We started with IV morphine and ketorolac, but I understand the ketorolac didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the morphine helps more with the pain. I’m glad we’re not using Compazine—I’m allergic to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted your allergies—Compazine, Dilaudid, and several others. We’re using promethazine instead for nausea, which should be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my G-tube is draining okay? I felt some relief after it was hooked up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it drained about 1,450 cc overnight—that’s a good amount. It helps reduce the pressure in your stomach and intestines. We’ll keep it to gravity for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I’ve been so worried about another blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But the imaging shows no blockage—just a lot of stool in the lower colon. No free air, so no sign of perforation. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my potassium? I saw it was low in the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 3.2, which is a bit low. We’re giving you potassium supplements in your IV fluids to bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve had that before. It makes me feel weak when it’s low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep monitoring it. Now, your liver enzymes are also a bit elevated—ALT and AST are higher than usual. We did an ultrasound this morning to check your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of my hepatitis C? I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely the main cause. The ultrasound showed fatty infiltration of the liver, which can happen with chronic hepatitis C. It doesn’t show cirrhosis or serious damage, but you should follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely, but it’s important to monitor. Fatty liver can progress if not managed. Your primary doctor or GI specialist can help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to follow up. What about my blood thinner? I’m on warfarin for my DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your INR was low—only 1.6—so you weren’t fully protected against clots. We’ve started you on Lovenox injections to bridge until your INR comes back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done that before. How long will I need the shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just until your INR is stable above 2. We’ll check it again tomorrow. Once it’s in range, you can go back to warfarin alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The pain is much less, and I haven’t felt nauseous since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your INR is now 2.2, which is in the safe range, so we’ll stop the Lovenox and continue warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on a soft diet. We’ll begin with clear liquids and advance as tolerated. Your G-tube can stay clamped for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really looking forward to eating something. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you from IV morphine to your regular oral morphine. You can still use the liquid form as needed for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like metoclopramide and ranitidine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart all your usual medications. We’ll make sure your discharge list matches what you were on before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You ate dinner last night without any issues, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much stronger. Am I going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. Your pain is controlled, you’re eating well, and your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any instructions for when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue eating small, moderate meals. Stay on your regular meds. Watch for worsening pain, vomiting, or inability to tolerate food—those would be reasons to call your doctor or return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver ultrasound results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your primary care doctor or GI specialist in the next two weeks to discuss the fatty liver changes and your hepatitis C.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I started vomiting bile last night—no blood—and the pain got worse. It feels just like my past bowel blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of sclerosing mesenteritis and recurrent obstructions. Did you try anything at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took extra Phenergan and morphine, but it didn’t help. I still passed gas, though, so I wasn’t completely blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good you’re still passing gas. We did a CT scan and a plain X-ray. The CT shows your duodenum is more dilated than before, suggesting a partial blockage, but contrast is moving through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a full blockage? But it feels just like the last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a partial or transient obstruction, related to your mesenteritis. We’ll keep you NPO for now, give IV fluids, and vent your stomach through the G-tube to relieve pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my warfarin? My INR was 5.0 in the ER—that’s high, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s elevated. We’re holding your warfarin for now in case we need any procedures. We’ll restart it when you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show mild dehydration and low potassium. We’re correcting that with IV fluids and supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been feeling a bit weak. Is the fatty liver on the CT related to my hepatitis C?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. But your liver enzymes are stable, and ammonia is normal, so it’s not causing your current symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better—bowel sounds are returning. We’re going to start clear liquids slowly and cap your G-tube to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go back on my regular meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your metoclopramide and misoprostol to help gut motility. Aciphex isn’t available here, so we’re using famotidine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating liquids well. We’re advancing to a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We scheduled a small bowel follow-through to check your motility. It’s a test where you drink contrast, and we watch it move through your intestines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it make me nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give anti-nausea meds beforehand. It’s important to see if your bowels are moving properly despite the structural changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the SBFT showed normal motility. The contrast reached the colon in 50 minutes, which is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I keep getting these blockage-like episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anatomy is altered from mesenteritis—dilated loops, tethering—but the function is okay. It’s likely transient partial obstructions due to inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to try restarting your home medications fully, including Lyrica and Lamictal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired and a bit confused since yesterday. Could that be from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We checked your liver and ammonia—both normal. We think the altered mental status is from restarting Lyrica and Lamictal at full dose too quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to hold Lyrica for now and reduce Lamictal to 25mg. We’ll increase slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been anxious and having trouble sleeping too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue trazodone and lorazepam as needed. Social work will also check in to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting TPN today. Nutrition feels it’s needed because you’re not meeting your needs by mouth, especially after the setback.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was hoping to avoid TPN. I’ve had complications before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But with your malnutrition and risk of further obstruction, TPN will help you heal and maintain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. We’re continuing TPN and your oral diet. We’ll keep monitoring your G-tube output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m having more pain again, and I vomited. My G-tube just drained over 1300cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. We’re going back to NPO and IV fluids. A new X-ray shows ileus, not a full obstruction. It should resolve with rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this going to keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating, I know. Your underlying condition makes you prone to these episodes. We’re adjusting your pain plan to avoid heavy IV opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ileus is improving. We’re restarting oral meds and will try clears again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray shows diffuse bowel distention—likely ileus again. We’ll hold oral intake for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired of being stuck in bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard. But your body needs time. We’re continuing TPN and will try liquids again when you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The distention is improving. We’re seeing better motility. We’ll try small sips of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. We’re advancing diet slowly. We’ve restarted warfarin at your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my Lyrica and Lamictal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted Lyrica at a lower dose—75mg twice daily—and increased Lamictal to 50mg. We’ll keep titrating up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-ray shows moderate fecal loading but no obstruction. We’re adding bisacodyl to help with bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated. Should I take more senna?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to bisacodyl for now. We’ll adjust as needed. Docusate will stay for softening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. We’re continuing TPN at home. Your gastroenterologist will follow up on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home on TPN. What if I have another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you clear instructions. If vomiting or severe pain returns, come back. Otherwise, keep your GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’re on oral pain meds—morphine SR and liquid as needed—and tizanidine for muscle spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need the G-tube venting at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you feel bloated or nauseous. Otherwise, keep it capped. Use Phenergan as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dry eyes from Sjogren’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending artificial tears. Pilocarpine isn’t available here, but your regular doctor can restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re being discharged today. Your vitals are stable, and you’re managing symptoms well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been a long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a setback, but you’ve recovered. Continue TPN, all meds, and follow up with your PCP and GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just hope I can avoid another hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all do. But now you know the signs. Don’t hesitate to reach out if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard too. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in last night with abdominal and chest pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Yesterday afternoon, my usual left upper belly pain got much worse. I took morphine, but it didn’t help much. Then I started vomiting dark green fluid—about two liters. And suddenly, I had this sharp chest pain that went from my back to the front and up to my jaw.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The chest pain wasn’t worse with breathing or movement? And you didn’t have shortness of breath or sweating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it wasn’t related to breathing. And I didn’t sweat or feel short of breath. But I felt hot. I’ve also been more tired than usual for weeks, and dizzy when I exercise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ve reviewed your CT scan. It shows a worsening partial small bowel obstruction due to strictures from your fibrosing mesenteritis. Your G-tube has also moved into the wrong position—past the stomach into the small bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So that’s why I’m so bloated and sick? Does that explain the chest pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your heart tests were normal—no heart attack. The chest pain likely came from the abdominal distension and referred pain. We’ll manage the obstruction first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now. You’ll get fluids and nutrition through your IV. We’ll also replace your G-tube to make sure it’s in the stomach so we can decompress your bowel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. The radiology team will do it. In the meantime, we’ll control your pain and nausea with IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on morphine for years. Is it safe to keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue it carefully. We’re also giving you pregabalin and trazodone like you take at home for nerve pain and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we just finished replacing your G-tube. It’s now correctly placed in the stomach. We’ve connected it to suction to help drain fluid and reduce pressure in your bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I already feel a little less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a positive sign. We’ll keep monitoring your output. If it stays high, we may need to start TPN—total parenteral nutrition—through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had TPN before. It’s okay, but I’d rather eat if I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try to get you back on food soon. But we have to be careful. Your bowel is still partially blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube output is still high, so we’re starting TPN today. It will give you all the nutrition you need while your bowel rests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also adjusting your thyroid medicine. Your TSH was low, so we’re reducing levothyroxine from 100 to 75 mcg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had hypothyroidism for years. That makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood count dropped a bit, but we think it’s from a recent infection. Everything else looks stable. No sign of infection now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had bronchitis a few weeks ago. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely. Your counts are starting to improve on their own, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try advancing your diet to full liquids tomorrow. Your G-tube output has decreased, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Can I have broth and juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, things like that. But we’ll watch closely. If your pain or output increases, we may need to stop and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on full liquids, but your G-tube output went up again. So we’re switching you back to NPO for a few days and continuing TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was hoping to eat more. Is the blockage still there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the obstruction is still present. We’re going to repeat the CT scan and possibly do an endoscopy to look at the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new CT shows the same partial obstruction. The bowel beyond the blockage looks healthy, no sign of ischemia. We’ve scheduled an upper endoscopy for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can they fix it during the scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the blockage is high up and tight. The gastroenterologist may not be able to pass the scope through. But we’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy was done. The scope couldn’t pass through the stricture. But we’re starting a new medicine—octreotide—to reduce your gastric secretions and G-tube output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a hormone injection that slows down your digestive secretions. We’ll give it three times a day. We hope it will help your bowel rest and reduce output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people get cramps or diarrhea, but we’ll monitor you. It’s often very helpful for patients like you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube output has decreased significantly since starting octreotide. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain is much better. I haven’t needed much morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to try advancing your diet again—this time to a low-fat regular diet in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the low-fat diet well. We’re turning off TPN today and keeping you on oral intake. Your G-tube will stay in but we’ll reduce suction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my warfarin? I noticed it went up to 7.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because TPN contains vitamin K, which counteracts warfarin. Now that you’re off TPN, we’re reducing it back to 5 mg daily. Your INR was 1.5 this morning—slightly low, but safe for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my thyroid dose stayed at 75 mcg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep it there. Your levels are now in a better range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a small episode of chest pain today, similar to when you were admitted. But your EKG was normal, and the pain went away after you passed gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It felt like pressure building up and then releasing. So it’s still related to the bowel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely due to temporary distension. As long as it resolves quickly and your heart tests are normal, we’re not concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable for days. Pain is at your baseline, no nausea, eating well. We’re planning for discharge in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue most of your home meds. We’re adding octreotide—three times a day under the skin. And we’re keeping your levothyroxine at 75 mcg and warfarin at 5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need a prescription for the octreotide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send it to your pharmacy. A nurse will teach you how to give the injections before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up is set with your gastroenterologist next week. They’ll monitor your obstruction and adjust treatment as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR? Should I get it checked soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your anticoagulation clinic will call you for a check within the week. Keep taking warfarin daily at the same time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll go home on a low-fat diet, your regular meds, and octreotide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad we got the G-tube fixed and the octreotide is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this was a good step forward. Call us if you have increasing pain, can’t keep food down, or have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve reviewed your records from the outside hospital. You came in because of swelling and pain in your left ankle after a fall, and your INR was very high—12.3. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. I twisted it two weeks ago. It got worse, and I kept falling. The pain was unbearable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on warfarin for blood clots, and your INR was too high, so you got vitamin K and FFP. We’ll monitor that closely. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad. I can’t put any weight on it. The boot helps, but I keep losing balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ortho looked at your X-ray. No new fracture—just a severe sprain on top of an old avulsion injury. Surgery isn’t needed. Rest, elevation, and the boot are key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m worried about falling again. I feel so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get physical therapy to help with stability. For now, we’re holding warfarin and will restart it once your INR is safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my nausea? I’ve felt sick since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Your labs are mostly stable, but we’re checking your abdomen. You’ve had bowel issues before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fibrosing mesenteritis. I’ve had 23 surgeries. My stomach gets blocked sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re concerned you might be developing another partial blockage. We’ll do a CT scan tomorrow to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan shows your stomach and duodenum are dilated—signs of a partial small bowel obstruction. It’s likely from adhesions, and possibly from the narcotics you’ve been taking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Does that mean surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery isn’t recommended right now. We’ll manage it conservatively—NPO, IV fluids, and your G-tube will be used for suction to decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no food at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll start TPN—nutrition through your port—to keep you nourished while your bowel rests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I’m scared of clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re bridging you with Lovenox until your INR is stable. We’ll restart warfarin at a higher dose later—7.5mg—because your levels have been hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’ve been dizzy. Is that from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You were a bit dehydrated and orthostatic. IV fluids should help. Your heart rate is high—around 106—but it’s likely from pain and deconditioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures flagged coagulase-negative staph, but it’s likely a contaminant. You’ve had no fever since admission, so we’re stopping vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in your case. It’s common with port access. We’ll keep it clean and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest KUB shows the obstruction is still there, but stable. We’re keeping the G-tube on suction. Any nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but less than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re continuing octreotide to reduce secretions. Once output drops, we’ll switch the G-tube to gravity drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CTA. No pulmonary embolism, but the images were limited. Your liver shows more fat than before, and you have portal hypertension signs. But no acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my hepatitis C?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Fibrosing mesenteritis and repeated surgeries also contribute. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR dropped too low after vitamin K. We’ve restarted warfarin and are bridging with Lovenox until it climbs back to a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on Lovenox the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just until your INR is therapeutic. Then we’ll stop it and continue warfarin at 7.5mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your TSH is elevated—5.6. Your levothyroxine dose was recently lowered, but now it seems too low. We’re increasing it to 88mcg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fatigue is common with high TSH. This adjustment should help. We’ll check it again after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 10.5, even though you had a guaiac-positive stool. No active bleeding signs, so we’re not transfusing. Outpatient colonoscopy is recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m always anemic. Is this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s consistent with your baseline. We’re monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s X-ray shows the bowel obstruction is improving. Fewer air-fluid levels. We’re going to start advancing your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids. If you tolerate it, we’ll move to soft foods. TPN will continue until you can eat enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept down apple juice and broth. Good job. We’re switching to full liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so hungry. When can I eat solid food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you do well today, we’ll try soft solids tomorrow. But go slow—your gut has been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now therapeutic. We’ve stopped Lovenox. You’re back on warfarin 7.5mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bleeding risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve increased both warfarin and levothyroxine, which can raise bleeding risk. That’s why you must get your INR checked soon after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
