conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating soft foods well. We’re discontinuing TPN today. Your G-tube is now on gravity drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. PT says you’re safer with the walker. Once your pain is controlled and diet is stable, we’ll plan discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a regular diet for two days with no nausea or pain. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My ankle still hurts, but the boot helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a chronic injury. Keep using the boot, elevate it, and avoid falls. We’ll send instructions for home care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home on octreotide injections, warfarin, and levothyroxine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Check your INR in a few days and see your PCP. Also schedule colonoscopy and thyroid follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: Discharge tomorrow. You’re stable, eating well, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Keep resting, take meds as directed, and call if you have swelling, severe pain, or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Here’s your discharge summary. INR check in two days, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re strong—you’ve been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been vomiting several times a day for about five days and have had diarrhea with undigested food. My stomach pain has gotten worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of fibrosing mesenteritis and multiple bowel obstructions, we’re concerned this could be another partial small bowel obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds familiar. I’ve had this before. Does that mean I can’t eat again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—to let your bowel rest. We’ll give you fluids and nutrition through your G-tube and IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G-tube has been draining a lot lately. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping it on suction to help decompress your stomach. It’s been draining 500 to 1200 mL daily, which makes sense with the obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I take it for blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 2.0 on admission—within the therapeutic range. We’ll keep monitoring it and adjust your warfarin dose as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another bleed like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be careful. For now, we’re continuing your home dose of 2.5 mg daily and will adjust based on labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we reviewed your abdominal X-ray from yesterday. It shows a normal bowel gas pattern—no signs of complete obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not fully blocked? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s still a partial obstruction, which is why we’re keeping you NPO and on G-tube suction for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need to stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It depends on how quickly your bowel recovers. We’ll monitor your symptoms and output. It could be several days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on total parenteral nutrition—TPN—through your port-a-cath since you haven’t been able to eat for over a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember TPN from last time. Will I need it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging for home TPN. You’ll continue it until your GI doctor clears you to restart oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I hope it doesn’t take too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain team reviewed your meds. We’re increasing your MS Contin to 30 mg twice daily for better pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling more drowsy. Is that from the morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll monitor you closely. If the drowsiness continues, we may need to reduce the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been more somnolent the past day. We’re reducing your MS Contin back to 15 mg twice daily—the dose you were on at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt too out of it. I’m glad we’re adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reduced your promethazine to three times a day. It can add to drowsiness, especially with narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll stick to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been low in the mornings—around 90s/60s—but you’re not symptomatic. We’re encouraging more fluids by mouth when you can tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit weak when I stand. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as you’re not dizzy or passing out, it’s okay. We’ll keep an eye on it. Staying hydrated will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started your TPN yesterday. It’s going well—no complications so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad something is helping me get nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 2.4 today. We’re increasing your warfarin to 5 mg daily to keep it in the therapeutic range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with the TPN and everything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re monitoring closely. Your labs are stable, and you’re not bleeding. It’s important to stay anticoagulated due to your DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube is showing signs of granulation tissue. We’ve scheduled a procedure with interventional radiology to replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that urgent? I’m already feeling weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not an emergency, but replacing it now prevents complications later. The procedure is quick and done under local anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube was successfully replaced today under CT guidance. It’s now functioning well and ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it go okay? I felt some pressure but not much pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it went smoothly. They cauterized some granulation tissue, and the new tube is secure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows no bowel obstruction. Your G-tube output has decreased to about 800 mL yesterday, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I might start eating soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not there yet, but it’s moving in the right direction. We’ll keep monitoring and discuss with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.2—perfect. We’ll keep your warfarin at 5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll need to follow up with my PCP for checks, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please schedule regular INR checks with your primary care or anticoagulation clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is much better, and you’re more alert. We’re switching your pain meds back to your home regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. Can I start trying liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk to GI about it. For now, we’re focusing on stabilizing your nutrition with TPN at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back with low bacterial count—less than 10,000 organisms/mL. No infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I might have a UTI. Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no antibiotics needed. Your symptoms are from the bowel issue, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray today shows no obstruction. Your bowel is recovering. We’re planning for discharge in the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue TPN at home, monitor your G-tube output, and follow up with your GI doctor about restarting food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your discharge meds. Warfarin is now 5 mg daily, and your short-acting morphine is available for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the promethazine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it no more than three times a day. We want to avoid drowsiness, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you home with home health support for TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please keep your appointments. Call us if you have increasing pain, vomiting, or signs of infection at the G-tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing why you came in. You've been having more abdominal pain and vomiting than usual, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I usually vomit about once a week, but now it’s several times a day. The pain in my upper abdomen is much worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of many abdominal surgeries and fibrosing mesenteritis, we’re concerned about another partial bowel obstruction. We’ve already checked a scan of your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is there a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan doesn’t show a clear obstruction. There’s a lot of stool in your colon, but no dilated small bowel loops. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now and use your G-tube for suction to help relieve pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But I’m worried about nutrition. I’ve been dependent on TPN before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of that. We’ll start IV fluids and monitor your labs. If you can’t tolerate oral intake soon, we’ll restart TPN. We also noticed your INR was high—6.8—so we’ve held your warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. I’ve had issues with that before. Too high and I bleed, too low and I clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll monitor it closely and adjust your anticoagulation as needed. For now, we’re focusing on your pain and nausea with IV morphine and promethazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a G-tube check today. It’s still in place and working, but there’s moderate stool buildup. We’re still not seeing signs of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. But I’ve noticed some leakage around the tube lately. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could mean the tube is starting to wear out or shift. We’ll keep an eye on it. If it worsens, we may need to replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another imaging study via your G-tube. The contrast went into your stomach fine, but we couldn’t clearly see the pigtail part of the tube. It might be outside the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not working right? That could explain the leakage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ve scheduled a procedure to replace it tomorrow. It’s routine and done under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the G-tube was successfully replaced this morning. The old one had an unformed pigtail, which likely caused the leakage. The new one is secure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I already feel a little better knowing it’s fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did an endoscopy yesterday. It was limited due to your anatomy, but we didn’t see any blockage in the upper GI tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. But I’m still not improving much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, and we’re concerned about your nutrition. Given your chronic malnutrition and lack of progress, we’re starting TPN tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a fever the last two days. We drew blood cultures, and they came back positive for coagulase-negative staph.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From my port-a-cath? I’ve had infections there before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it appears to be a line infection. The good news is it’s not MRSA—it’s MRSE, which responds to vancomycin. We’re starting IV vancomycin and will also do lock therapy on the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two weeks. We’ll finish the course here, but you’ll need follow-up blood cultures after discharge to make sure it’s fully cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a small bowel follow-through today. It shows your duodenum and proximal jejunum are very dilated, with a transition point likely due to adhesions—scar tissue from past surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s causing the blockage? Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery isn’t recommended right now. You’ve had 23 abdominal surgeries already, and the risk is too high. We’ll continue managing this conservatively with TPN and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s just frustrating to keep dealing with this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re also starting amitriptyline for chronic pain and methylnaltrexone to help with bowel motility, since narcotics can slow things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today was clear, no pneumonia. But we noticed a small lucent lesion in your left clavicle. It looks benign—possibly a cyst—but we recommend monitoring it clinically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any pain there. Should I get an MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if it becomes painful. For now, just watch it. No urgent action needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are now negative. The vancomycin is working. We’ll finish the two-week course and plan for discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. What about my anticoagulation? My INR was low earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we tried increasing your warfarin, but your INR didn’t respond. Because of your history of supratherapeutic INRs, we’ve switched you to enoxaparin, a daily injection, which is safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can manage that at home. Will I need it long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes, due to your history of DVT. Your primary doctor will help decide long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line today so you can finish your antibiotics safely. The port-a-cath is still infected, so we’ll use this for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram to rule out endocarditis from the bloodstream infection. Good news—it shows no sign of infection on your heart valves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focusing on transitioning your pain control from IV to oral morphine. We’re using a more concentrated form so you take less volume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on morphine for years. I hope this works as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re matching your previous dose. You’ll also continue octreotide and misoprostol as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. TPN is cycling nightly at home, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with home health. I’m glad I won’t have to stay in the hospital for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also arranged for an IV iron infusion before discharge to address your iron deficiency anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been feeling more fatigued lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube fell out this morning, didn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, during the night. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already replaced it using fluoroscopy. The tract was still open, so it went smoothly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That was fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final blood cultures are negative. The infection is cleared. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue TPN nightly, take enoxaparin twice daily, and use oral morphine as needed. You’ll also take promethazine syrup for nausea. We’ll send home supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the follow-up cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one set this week and another in a week. Your primary team will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge. We’ll send your TPN and nursing setup with you, and you’ll follow up with your GI and primary doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything. It’s been a long stay, but I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. We’re glad we could help stabilize you. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your G-tube site should be kept clean and dry. Watch for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve done this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep taking your levothyroxine and other regular meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t miss those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a summary to your doctors so they’re up to date.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I appreciate the coordination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team will make sure everything’s set. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with fevers. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had low-grade fevers for a few days—around 99 to 101. I also feel chills every day around 4 p.m. and pain near my port site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of port-related infections. We’ve drawn blood cultures, and one came back positive for coagulase-negative staph. It’s likely the source of your fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That happened before. Is it serious? Could it spread?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking it seriously. It can lead to complications like endocarditis, so we’ll do an echocardiogram to check your heart valves. But the good news is this type of staph is usually treatable with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel a little better. What about my port and PICC? Should they stay in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given this is a recurrence, and you’ve had multiple line infections, we recommend removing both the port and PICC to eliminate the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. How will I get my TPN then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a new PICC line once the infection clears. It’ll be saline-locked to reduce infection risk. You’ll still get your TPN through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And the antibiotics? Will I be on them long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll need four weeks of IV vancomycin. We’ve already started your first dose in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed your port this morning. The culture from the tip confirmed coagulase-negative staph, so we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to remove it so soon after the last infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because we’ve confirmed the infection source. Leaving it in would risk treatment failure. We’ll wait for your blood cultures to clear before placing a new line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative—great news. But you developed new abdominal pain yesterday. Can you describe it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sharp, in my upper left side, different from my usual pain. It started suddenly and hasn’t let up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray, and it shows a dilated loop in your small bowel. It could be a partial obstruction from adhesions. We’ll get a CT to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many surgeries—could the adhesions be getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. Your fibrosing mesenteritis causes chronic inflammation and scarring. Surgery isn’t an option now, so we’ll manage this medically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows wall thickening and fluid around the jejunum, plus a narrowing—consistent with partial mechanical obstruction from adhesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous? Could it turn into a full blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Right now, it’s partial—contrast passes through. We’ll keep you on bowel rest, use your G-tube for decompression, and give IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube has been leaking a bit. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. It might be pulled out slightly. We’ll arrange to replace it to prevent infection and ensure proper drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube replacement went well. The old one was partially dislodged, which explains the leakage. The new one is secure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My pain is still bad—can we do more for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted pain management. We’re trying a combination of oral morphine, gabapentin, and amitriptyline. We’ll also try a lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on a PCA before—why not now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because when you were switched to oral morphine earlier, your pain worsened despite higher doses. The pain team thinks there may be a psychological component, so we’re being cautious with opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also concerned about your mood. You mentioned feeling hopeless. Can we talk about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is constant. I’ve thought about not wanting to go on. My therapist is worried too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you’re honest. Psychiatry evaluated you and agrees your pain is the main driver. They don’t think you need inpatient psych, but we’ll keep supporting you here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an enteroscopy today to look for a source of pain. The bowel looks inflamed but no blockage or ulcers. It’s likely functional pain from your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing shows up, but the pain is real?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. The pain is real. But sometimes, chronic pain changes how the nervous system works. That’s why we’re using nerve medications like gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function dipped—creatinine went up to 1.2. We think it’s from dehydration due to high G-tube output and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my kidneys be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with aggressive IV fluids, it’s improving. We’ll keep you on maintenance IVs to match your losses and prevent this from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another CT with contrast. The duodenum is still dilated, but no leak or worsening obstruction. The G-tube is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try eating anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried a soft diet, but it increased your G-tube output and pain. You’re not absorbing nutrients. You’ll need to stay on full liquids, TPN, and IV fluids at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t eat normally ever again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your bowel is too damaged. But we’ll work with your GI specialist to see if things improve over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stool tests came back negative for C. diff and other infections. So your symptoms aren’t from a new gut infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about my anemia? I feel so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you an iron infusion and one unit of blood before the endoscopy. Your levels improved. We’ll keep you on oral iron and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echocardiogram was clear—no vegetations, no endocarditis. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was so worried about that. Thank you for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve completed two weeks of vancomycin. Since your cultures remain negative, we’ll continue for another two weeks to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then I can get a new port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but only after we confirm the infection is gone with follow-up blood cultures. We’ll also consider a special ethanol lock to prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is better with the new meds. You’re down to oral morphine and gabapentin. How are you feeling overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still uncomfortable, but more manageable. I’m glad the nausea is improving with the Zofran and ginger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re weaning off IV anti-nausea meds. You can use lorazepam and promethazine by mouth now, with Zofran for breakthrough nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function has normalized. We’re switching from continuous IV fluids to bolus doses three times a week to improve your quality of life.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds great. Less tied to the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final vancomycin dose is tomorrow. Blood cultures are negative. You’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue TPN, full liquids, and bolus IV fluids. Take your new meds: gabapentin, amitriptyline, and increased octreotide. Watch for fever or G-tube issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Get them drawn in two weeks. If negative, you can see Dr. Patel about replacing your port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been a long stay, but I feel safer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. We’ll make sure you have home health, physical therapy, and close follow-up. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in. Your labs are stable, you’re walking well, and your pain is controlled. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. I’ll miss the team, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll miss you too. But you’re stronger now. Keep in touch with your doctors, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right, everything’s signed. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. For everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to take your medications as prescribed and keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if you have any fever or increased pain, don’t wait—call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve handled this incredibly well. Proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged home health to help with your PICC and TPN. They’ll visit regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll feel more confident with support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your pain clinic will adjust your meds. Don’t hesitate to reach out if pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind. I’m feeling more hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best outcome. Take care, and we’re always here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were transferred here last night with right upper quadrant pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It started suddenly—like a sharp pinch—after I reached for something. Then it got worse, radiating around my side to my back. It’s different from my usual pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And does anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sitting up with my knees bent helps. Lying flat makes it worse. I’ve also been nauseous and dry heaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned no fever or chills, and your labs don’t show infection. We did a chest X-ray, which showed some small bowel dilation but no lung issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I refused the CT scan yesterday. I’ve had so many. Is it really necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Given your history and normal liver enzymes, we’re leaning away from gallbladder or liver causes. No signs of kidney stones either on ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be musculoskeletal—like a strained muscle from reaching. The pain pattern fits. We’ll treat it with Toradol and morphine for now and see how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been on TPN and my regular meds—should I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your home regimen: octreotide, gabapentin, morphine, and the others. We’ve restarted TPN and liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my port—can I get it replaced soon? I just finished antibiotics for the last infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need to wait for blood cultures to confirm no current infection. You had another line infection recently, so we want to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I remember. I just hope this pain isn’t another complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. For now, we’ll focus on pain control and hydration. A social worker will also check in to help coordinate your support services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your urine culture came back—showed mixed flora, so likely contamination. No UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So nothing there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And your blood work is stable—no infection markers. We’re sticking with the musculoskeletal idea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not another infection. But the pain is still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added warm packs and adjusted your morphine. Let’s give it another day to see if it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still sharp, but less intense. The warm packs help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’ll keep the current plan. Your TPN is running well, and your G-tube is functioning normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my pilocarpine and eye drops—my mouth and eyes are still dry, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep those up for your Sjogren’s. And your Lovenox injections are scheduled twice daily for your clotting history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been getting those. No swelling in my arms or legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll continue monitoring. Let’s aim to reduce IV meds and transition fully to oral pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You’re looking more comfortable today. Pain improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I only needed one dose of morphine last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll switch you to oral morphine concentrate and reduce IV use. Still no fever or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, both are gone. I even had a small bowel movement yesterday—hard, but something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your GI motility is still slow, but we’re not seeing obstruction. We’ll keep Miralax and Colace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gabapentin and amitriptyline for nerve pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue those. They help with chronic pain and sleep. We’re also keeping your antidepressants—Lamictal, trazodone, and Ativan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been feeling less anxious since being here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Pain is much better, and no new issues have come up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the blood cultures? Any results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One set showed coagulase-negative staph, but it’s likely a skin contaminant. Other bottles show no growth. We don’t think it’s a true infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at this time. Since you just finished a course, and cultures are mostly negative, we’ll hold off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my port? Can I get it replaced?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once Dr. ___ confirms the cultures are fully clear, you can schedule the placement. Discuss it with her at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call her. What about my meds? Any changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re simplifying a few. Amitriptyline is reduced to 25mg, gabapentin to 300mg three times a day. Others stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can manage that. And TPN at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue as before. Weekly labs while on TPN—please fax results to the number we gave you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’re finalizing your discharge. You’re doing well—pain is mild, you’re eating, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: follow up with Dr. ___ for culture results and port placement. Resume all home services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And call if pain worsens or I get a fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Otherwise, we expect continued improvement. You’re cleared to go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch if anything changes, but all looks good for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge meds and instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re glad we could help get your pain under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. It’s been a rough few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But you’re strong, and your team is here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand your PICC line stopped working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I just got home two days ago and noticed a little blood around the site. Then I couldn’t flush it at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you pull on it or change the dressing yourself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t touch it. I just tried to flush it like I always do, and it wouldn’t go through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. The ER team examined it and found one of the ports was cracked, so they removed it. We’re sending it for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. But why am I being admitted again so soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because one of the blood cultures drawn from the line showed some bacteria—gram-positive cocci in clusters. It could be a contaminant, but we need to treat it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I don’t have a fever or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. No fever, chills, or other symptoms suggest it might not be a full infection. But since you rely on TPN, we can’t take chances with your line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on IV vancomycin to cover the bacteria. We’re also waiting on more blood cultures to see if it’s growing elsewhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin? I’ve had that before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your kidney function and check levels of the drug. Some people get red man syndrome—flushing or itching—but we can slow the infusion if that happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also need to place a new PICC line once we’re sure the blood is clear. But not until your cultures are negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they had trouble with my veins. Is that going to be an issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your records show stenosis in the right brachiocephalic vein. The interventional radiology team will use ultrasound guidance and may need special wires, but they’ve done this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I just want to get back on TPN soon. My stomach hasn’t been great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart TPN as soon as the new line is in. In the meantime, you’re getting fluids and your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my pain is the same—still chronic RUQ. Nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I reviewed your last admission. We’ll keep you on morphine concentrate as needed and continue octreotide for your fibromatosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my psychiatrist wanted me to try a clonidine patch instead of Ativan. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve ordered the 0.1 mg patch weekly. We’ll start that tomorrow. It may help with anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That’s a good sign—the bacteria may have just been from the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So does that mean I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your infectious disease specialist wants you to complete two weeks of vancomycin, just to be safe, especially since the PICC tip wasn’t cultured.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So we’re still waiting on the new line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, scheduled for tomorrow morning. The team will place it in your right brachial vein. It might take a bit longer due to the narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any prep I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just nothing to eat or drink after midnight. We’ll hold your Lovenox in the morning and restart it after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The PICC was successfully placed in your right brachial vein. It took some maneuvering, but the tip is in the SVC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Can I start TPN now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s already being set up. We’ll also resume your home meds through the line as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin continues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily. We checked a trough level yesterday—it was 14, which is good. We’ll keep monitoring weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other labs? Blood counts okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is stable at 11, white count normal. No signs of infection or anemia worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. ID clinic confirmed: continue vancomycin for two weeks. They’ll follow your levels and blood work weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get the infusion at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home health will set that up. You’ll also need weekly labs sent to your ID doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? Still the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, morphine concentrate as needed, Zofran, Phenergan. We increased amitriptyline to 50 mg at night for nerve pain and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And trazodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now 150 mg at night. We’re adjusting for better sleep and mood support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and your new PICC is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your ID doctor soon. Continue vancomycin for two weeks. Weekly labs—CBC, chem 10, vancomycin levels—faxed to their office.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And home health for the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll coordinate. Also resume your support services—nursing, nutrition, social work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I notice redness or swelling at the PICC site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your team immediately. Also if you develop fever, chills, or can’t flush the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my sons are being checked for MEN syndrome. Should they be worried about this infection risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This was likely related to your line and medical history. It’s not genetic. But they should inform their doctors about your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll let them know. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you were admitted because of a positive blood culture from your PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My infectious disease doctor sent me in. It was coagulase-negative staph, but only one bottle grew it. I’ve had this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important context. Given your history of serious line infections, we’re taking this seriously even if it’s just one bottle. You don’t have fever or chills now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel stable. My pain and nausea are about my usual baseline—still high, but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. We’ll remove the PICC line as a precaution and start you on antibiotics just in case. We’ll also draw more blood cultures to make sure nothing else shows up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still get my TPN? I can’t eat normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on peripheral nutrition for now—PPN—until we get a new central line placed. Nutrition team is involved and will help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’m worried about my access. Last time, they couldn’t get into my arms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware. The vascular access team will evaluate you tomorrow. We may need to consider other options if the upper arms aren’t viable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All your repeat blood cultures are negative so far, and the PICC tip didn’t grow anything. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t a real infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out completely. Sometimes only one culture catches it. Infectious disease still recommends treating it as a possible line infection, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the new line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for a PICC attempt tomorrow. They’ll use ultrasound to try the right arm. If that fails, we have a backup plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got clots before. Could that be blocking access?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We ordered a Doppler ultrasound. We’ll know more by tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed a non-occlusive clot in your right subclavian vein. That explains why access has been hard. It’s not blocking flow completely, but it limits options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the PICC won’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll still try, but the risk of failure is higher. If it doesn’t work, we may need to place a tunneled line in your groin—the femoral vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: In my leg? Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s less ideal than upper body lines because of higher infection risk, but for patients like you with limited access, it’s a valid option. The team will take every precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my spinal stimulator—could that be involved? I heard you were checking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT to check for infection around the leads. No fluid collection or signs of infection. Neurosurgery says it’s safe to leave it in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I rely on it for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The PICC team tried earlier—they got into the basilic vein but couldn’t advance the line far enough. The tip ended up in the axillary vein, not central. It’s not suitable for long-term TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll proceed with the tunneled femoral line. Interventional radiology will do it tomorrow. It’s a more permanent solution with a lower risk of dislodgement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to walk with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you’ll need to keep the site clean and dry. Home nursing will help you with care, and a visiting service will manage your TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the femoral line was placed successfully this morning. The tip is in the upper vena cava, and it’s flowing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start TPN again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s already ordered. Nutrition will restart your usual formula. We’ll also resume your home meds as they were.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics? Do I still need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infectious disease reviewed your case. Since cultures cleared and the old line was removed, you don’t need antibiotics. The concern was low-grade, and no ongoing infection was found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I was worried about another long course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you one more day to make sure the line is working and you’re stable. Then we can plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I follow up with ID?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They want to do a PFGE test on the old and new staph cultures to see if it’s the same strain. Could help determine if there’s a hidden source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like a biofilm somewhere?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But nothing showed up on imaging. Still, they want to be thorough given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’ve scheduled your discharge for later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will visit to help with line care and TPN. You’ll continue all your usual medications. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever at the line site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube and pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All unchanged. Keep using the G-tube for venting as needed. Your pain regimen stays the same—morphine, gabapentin, amitriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I should talk to my GI doctor about other nutrition options, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. With your access challenges, it’s worth discussing long-term alternatives. But for now, the femoral line is the safest way to deliver your TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have my follow-up with GI and ID in two weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both are scheduled. Please keep those appointments. Call us sooner if you develop any signs of infection or line issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing we have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A nurse will go over everything with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in with right-sided chest pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started yesterday morning. It’s sharp and gets worse when I breathe deeply or move. It’s been getting stronger since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, cough, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or trouble breathing. Just the pain and this ongoing nausea I’ve had for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history and the pain, we did a CT scan of your chest to check for blood clots or fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was anything found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—no blood clot in your lungs. But we did find a small fracture in your fifth rib on the right side, near the front. It looks a few days old.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A rib fracture? But I didn’t fall or get hit. Could it be from vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very possible. Severe or repeated vomiting can strain the chest muscles and even cause rib fractures. That might explain why the pain is higher than the fracture site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been vomiting a lot lately. What about my line? Should we be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood from your femoral tunneled line, and the culture came back positive for Enterococcus avium, a type of bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no—not another line infection. Do I need it removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted Infectious Disease. They don’t think removal is necessary this time. We’ll treat it with antibiotics and a special lock solution in the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting daptomycin, given through your line once a day. It covers this type of bacteria well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lock solution?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Originally, we planned to use ethanol, but there’s a shortage. So we’ll use vancomycin instead—put in the line for two hours before each TPN session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can manage that at home with help. Will I need this for long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home on daptomycin for 10 more days. A nurse will come to give it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain? Morphine helps a little, but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Toradol, an anti-inflammatory, to help with the rib and muscle pain. But we’ll only use it short-term because of your stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s smart. I’ve had gastritis before. What about my TPN? My G-tube output has been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GI doctor thinks the high output suggests a partial blockage. We’ve restarted TPN to support your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll need that at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same as before—through your femoral line. We’ll coordinate home care for TPN, antibiotics, and the vancomycin locks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are all negative—no bacteria growing from your IV or line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean the infection is clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign. The single positive culture likely came from the line. With treatment, we expect it to resolve fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You rated it 5 out of 10 this morning—down from 8. The Toradol seems to be helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’ve been a bit nauseous since starting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expected that. We’ll stop Toradol today and rely more on morphine. We don’t want to risk stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are continuing as before. We adjusted gabapentin and lamotrigine doses slightly based on your weight and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show stable kidney function and mild anemia, which you’ve had before. White count is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any update on the bacteria?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The final sensitivity report shows the Enterococcus is sensitive to daptomycin, vancomycin, and ampicillin. We’re confident in your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel better already. Pain is down to a 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on track for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat blood cultures remain negative. Infectious Disease confirms you can finish daptomycin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin lock?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that before each TPN session. A nurse will show your caregiver how to do it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Infectious Disease in one week. Also, get blood work—CBC, basic metabolic panel, and CK—before that visit and fax the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still present but at your usual level. We didn’t find any new obstruction or acute issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared for discharge today. You’ve improved significantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue daptomycin daily for 10 days, use vancomycin lock before TPN, take your regular meds, and monitor for fever or redness at the line site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your morphine as needed. Most rib fractures heal in 4–6 weeks with rest and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much more comfortable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The home health team will arrive before noon to set everything up. We’ll also send your records to your specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge summary mentions the rib fracture and line infection as main issues. All other conditions are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I read it. Everything looks accurate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will go over your meds one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready whenever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have you out within the hour. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with the plan and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You were brought in after having shaking episodes and trouble speaking. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I had one of my usual shaking spells, but this time it lasted much longer. And then I couldn’t speak—just couldn’t get the words out. It scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had these shaking episodes before—called pseudoseizures—and they usually don’t last long. This time was different. Did you feel weak or numb? Any headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No headache. Just the shaking and then the speech trouble. It’s better now, but I’m worried—could this be a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a head CT scan, and I’m happy to tell you there’s no sign of a stroke, bleed, or mass. That’s very reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But why did this happen? Is it related to my infection or the daptomycin I’m on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that. Daptomycin can rarely affect the nervous system, but it’s not common. Your neuro exam is normal now, and your speech came back by 7 a.m. We think this may be related to stress or a conversion-type reaction, especially given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a seizure or stroke, but something else? I’ve been under a lot of stress with the pain and the line infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your symptoms are real, but they don’t match a typical seizure or neurological injury. Stress and chronic illness can sometimes cause symptoms like this. We’ll keep monitoring you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. Your liver enzymes were a bit high when you arrived—ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase—but they’re already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the daptomycin? Should we stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Daptomycin can affect the liver, but your levels are only mildly elevated and coming down. We’ve spoken with Infectious Disease—they agree to continue it since you’re treating a serious line infection with Enterococcus avium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s safe. My rib pain is still bad—can I get something stronger? Morphine helps, but I asked for Dilaudid before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you prefer Dilaudid, but you have a history of GI issues, and stronger opioids can worsen that. We’ll stick with morphine for now, and we’ll keep an eye on your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust you. What about my blood thinner? I’m on Lovenox for my DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PTT was high when you arrived, but it normalized quickly. No sign of bleeding, and your kidney function is fine. We’re continuing Lovenox 80 mg twice daily as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. Your symptoms have resolved, labs are stable, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already have blood work scheduled soon—we’re adding liver function tests to that draw. And one blood culture is still pending; your ID team will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking daptomycin and the vancomycin lock for my line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Continue the IV daptomycin daily and the vancomycin antibiotic lock twice a day in your femoral line. And keep all your other home medications, including TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the speech trouble or shaking happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s prolonged or you’re concerned, go to the ER. But given what we’ve seen, it’s likely related to stress. Your neurologic workup was clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in. You’re doing well, and we’re cleared for discharge. Home health will assist with your IV meds and TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. I’ll follow up with my doctors and get those labs done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just waiting for the discharge papers. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re discharged with services. Rest well, and we’ll see you in follow-up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You came in because of dark-brown drainage from your G-tube. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up around 4:30 this morning and noticed the fluid in the bag was dark brown, almost reddish. It’s usually greenish-yellow. I’ve had bleeding before, so I got worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good call. We checked a sample in the ER and it was guaiac positive, which means there’s blood. You’re on Lovenox for your history of blood clots—this could make bleeding more likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ve been on Lovenox for my upper arm clots. But I don’t feel dizzy or weak. My blood pressure should be okay, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your vitals are stable—blood pressure 116/82, heart rate 93. We drew blood, and your hemoglobin was 10.2, which is a bit low but not a big drop from your baseline. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. But why is this happening now? I had an EGD not too long ago and they said everything looked okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did. The last one showed some irritation and redness around the G-tube site, but no active bleeding. We think this might be related to that irritation, possibly worsened by the anticoagulant.
