conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a new ulcer or something serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we know yet. The GI team wants to do another endoscopy to make sure. We’ll schedule that for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my TPN? I haven’t had it since this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding TPN for now since we’re checking for bleeding. Nutrition team is involved, and you’ll restart it at home with your usual 12-hour cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? I’ve been off morphine at home, but my belly’s been sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you some IV Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, but we’re not continuing it after discharge. You’re still on gabapentin and amitriptyline, which help with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I don’t want to get dependent again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. Also, social work mentioned you had some thoughts about not wanting to go on. Can you talk about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was overwhelmed in the ER. With everything—the pain, the bleeding, the tubes. I said things I didn’t mean. I’m not suicidal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. Psychiatry saw you and agreed you’re safe. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re cleared for regular care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just need to get through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—we ran blood cultures and they came back with no growth. No sign of infection in your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about that Enterococcus infection from my femoral line? Am I still on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed the daptomycin course. Infectious disease reviewed it and said no further IV antibiotics are needed. You’ll keep the vancomycin lock for the line, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s one less thing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed Streptococcus anginosus. It’s likely a contaminant or low-grade UTI, but since you’re not running a fever or feeling sick, we’re not treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll watch it, but it’s probably not related to your current issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood work shows your hemoglobin is stable at 10.9. No further drop. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. When’s the endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for 9 a.m. You’ll be sedated, and the doctor will look for the source of the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy is done. Good news—no active bleeding. There’s mild gastritis around the G-tube site, and some old blood, but nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just irritation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We think the G-tube is causing some chronic irritation, and the Lovenox may have triggered a small bleed. But it’s healed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a new tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The site looks clean, no infection. We’ll keep monitoring. You’ll go back to your regular ranitidine—no PPIs due to your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, omeprazole gave me kidney issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Ranitidine should help reduce stomach acid and protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain’s manageable. G-tube output is still brown, but less than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. It’ll clear over the next few days as the old blood drains out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Lovenox? Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re keeping it. Your history of upper extremity clots is serious. The benefit outweighs the small bleeding risk, especially now that the bleeding has stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go home with your regular medications and restart TPN with home health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. Same doses of gabapentin, amitriptyline, ranitidine, levothyroxine, and the rest. You’ll also keep the vancomycin lock for your line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sending it home with you. Use your oral morphine if needed, but try the other pain meds first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, no active bleeding, and your labs are consistent with your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your home health team to restart TPN. If the G-tube output becomes bright red or you feel lightheaded, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you had a small bowel endoscopy today as part of your evaluation. It was unremarkable, no source of bleeding found beyond the mild stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. This was likely a small, self-limited bleed from G-tube irritation. With your history, we wanted to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll document everything for your follow-up team. You’re cleared to leave once the discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep an eye on your mood. If you feel overwhelmed again, please reach out. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reviewed your hepatitis C—it’s stable, no liver issues now. Continue your usual monitoring with your specialist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment next month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay on track with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in today from the GI clinic because of severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain is constant, all over my belly, and it’s been above 10 out of 10 for weeks. Nothing at home helps—especially not the morphine. Only IV Dilaudid gives any relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned nausea and vomiting too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, constant nausea. I stopped my TPN three weeks ago because it made me sicker, but the nausea didn’t go away. I’ve lost about 20 pounds since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. We’ll get you started on hospital TPN to help with nutrition. We also want to manage your pain better. We’ll consult the chronic pain team to help adjust your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just need something that works. I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. We’ll do everything we can. For now, we’ll keep you on your current meds and monitor your labs and vitals closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your albumin is 3.0, which is low but better than the 2.0 from outside. Your hemoglobin is 10.9, so no active bleeding. We’ve started you on IV TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the TPN going to make me nauseous again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using a different formula than your home one—closer to what you’ve tolerated in the hospital before. We’ll monitor you closely and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll give it a try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chronic pain team met with you yesterday. Starting today, we’re increasing your gabapentin to 900 mg three times a day and amitriptyline to 100 mg at night. We’re also starting a Dilaudid PCA pump for 24 hours to see if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried so many things. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to find what works best for you. The PCA lets you control the dose safely. We’ll reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You mentioned new pain and swelling on your left thigh this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s tender and hard. I’ve had cords there from Lovenox shots, but this feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ordering an ultrasound to check for a clot or other issue. Given your anticoagulation, we’re concerned about a hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. No DVT, which is good. But there are two fluid collections in your thigh—could be abscesses or hematomas. You’re not febrile, so infection seems less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery reviewed it and recommends conservative care—warm compresses, lidocaine patches, and monitoring. We’ve held your Lovenox for now because your factor Xa level was high—suggesting you were over-anticoagulated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not on Lovenox anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched to a lower, prophylactic dose—40 mg once daily—since you have a history of DVTs. This balances bleeding and clotting risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your thigh swelling is already a bit smaller today. Pain improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the warm and cold packs help, and the lidocaine patch too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that up. Your nausea has also improved—from constant to about 3 out of 10. You’re tolerating clear liquids well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the nausea is better. The TPN isn’t making me sick, which is a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried the Fentanyl patch yesterday, but you said it made you feel strange?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I felt foggy and had bad thoughts—like I didn’t want to be here. I know it’s not safe, so I told the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for speaking up. We stopped the patch because of your history with suicidal ideation on opioids. We’ve switched to buprenorphine, but you said it didn’t help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No relief at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re now starting methadone 5 mg twice daily. It may help where others haven’t. We’ll monitor closely for side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try anything at this point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped to 8.4, but it’s stable now. We’re attributing it to chronic anemia from malabsorption. You’re on iron, and we’ll check your CBC after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. It’s been low before. We’re watching it, and your primary doctor will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The TPN company has replicated the hospital formula for your home use. You’ll restart it at home with the new mix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it works. I can’t afford to lose more weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is still significant, but methadone seems to be helping a bit. The chronic pain team feels it’s the best option now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not perfect, but better than nothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also starting a lidocaine patch for your leg pain and ketoconazole cream for a groin rash you mentioned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My skin’s been itchy too—any idea why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be from dryness or Sjogren’s. We’re keeping Benadryl available if it bothers you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well overall. The hematoma is shrinking, your pain is more manageable, and you’re tolerating nutrition. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What changes will I have at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on methadone twice daily instead of morphine, gabapentin and amitriptyline at higher doses, and Lovenox 40 mg once daily. We’re switching from vancomycin to ethanol dwell for your catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the ethanol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps prevent infections and works better with your TPN. The home team will show you how.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also want to check your CBC the day after discharge. Your hemoglobin was low, so we need to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still in pain, but it’s better than when I came in. I’m glad to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve made several medication changes. Let me go over them again so you’re clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on methadone for pain, higher doses of gabapentin and amitriptyline, and Lovenox once daily. You’ll use the ethanol catheter dwell and the new TPN formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lidocaine patch for my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, apply it at night for 12 hours. The thigh bruise is healing but may take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if pain worsens, you develop fever, or the leg swelling returns. Follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll send your discharge instructions and prescriptions to your home team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest at home and keep up with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re improving. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep those appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Let us know if anything comes up before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s our job. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with fever and chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a low-grade fever at home, up to 100.1, and I’ve been feeling achy and sweaty. It feels just like my past line infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We noticed some redness and a small amount of pus around your left femoral line. That’s definitely concerning. We’ve started you on IV vancomycin just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had these infections before—usually from the line. But I’m also nauseous and throwing up more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you some IV promethazine for the nausea. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your blood work shows your white count is normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t been on my methadone lately—it wasn’t helping my pain. I’ve been using the Dilaudid PCA instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your home pain meds—amitriptyline, gabapentin, clonidine—and keep the PCA for now. We’ll talk to the pain team about adjusting things if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And please let the ID and pain services know I’m here. I’m on Lovenox too, for my history of clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Already done. We’re continuing your Lovenox. We’re also monitoring your hemoglobin—it’s stable so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia for a while. I’m on iron. Is my TPN going to be paused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re holding TPN for now because of the possible line infection. We don’t want to feed any bacteria. You can have regular food as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I can eat a little. But I’m worried—could this be serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. The redness and pus suggest the line might be infected. We drew blood cultures and sent a catheter tip for testing once it’s removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace the line with a new one on the right side. But first, we wanted to check your veins with an MRV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I can’t have an MRI. I have a spinal stimulator for pain. They said it’s not safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right—we confirmed that. So we’ll go ahead with replacing the line without the MRV. Interventional Radiology will place a new tunneled catheter in your right femoral vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I trust them. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—Dilaudid and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed but may remember parts of it. It’s usually well tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative so far. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Any other tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray was clear—no pneumonia. We’re also watching your electrolytes and kidney function. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve felt a bit better today—no fever, and the nausea is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep the vancomycin going until after the line is replaced, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling the line replacement for tomorrow morning. Any questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they remove the old line completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll remove the left femoral line and send the tip for culture. Then place the new one on the right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my TPN—when can I restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait a few days after the new line is in and we’re sure there’s no infection. We don’t want to risk seeding the new line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll manage with food and IV fluids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. You’re still doing well—no fever, labs stable. The procedure is set for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m feeling okay. A bit anxious about the procedure, but I know it’s necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. The team is experienced, and you’ll be sedated. We’ll be right there with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. The procedure went smoothly. They removed the old line—there was a bit of pus in the tunnel—and placed the new one in your right groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember some pressure, but not much pain. Is the old line being tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tip was sent for culture. We’ll get results in a few days. For now, we’ll keep you on antibiotics until we’re confident it’s clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? Can I keep the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. But we’ll taper it off before discharge. We’ll keep your regular meds—amitriptyline, gabapentin, clonidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad we’re addressing the line. I’ve had too many infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking every precaution. The new site is clean, and we’ll teach you how to care for it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your catheter tip culture came back with no growth. No bacteria found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief! Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. We’ll stop the vancomycin since there’s no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart it at home through the new line. Be sure to follow your usual sterile technique.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your regular list—no changes. We’ve given you a printed copy. Continue Lovenox, pain meds, and everything else as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get fever or redness at the new site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER. Watch for redness, swelling, or drainage. Otherwise, follow up with your primary team in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping manage your care today. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. Honestly, I’m in a lot of pain—more than usual. It’s that same crampy, colicky feeling, but worse on the right side. I threw up about two liters of greenish fluid last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned this has been going on for a while, but this episode was worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I usually vomit a few times a day, but not this much. And my G-tube isn’t helping like it used to. They switched me to a smaller, more flexible one, and it just doesn’t drain well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from this morning. It shows that the loops of your small bowel are more dilated than before—about 5 to 6 centimeters—which suggests your chronic partial bowel obstruction may be a bit worse right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So it’s not a new blockage, just the old one acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s the same area, likely in the left lower quadrant, just a little more distended. Surgery was consulted, and they agree no operation is needed at this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough surgeries. What’s the plan then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your bowel rest. You’ll get IV fluids, and we’ll restart your TPN through your femoral line once we’re sure things are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for pain? I know my usual ER protocol is up to 1 mg of IV Dilaudid over an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s still the plan. We’ll start with 0.25 mg every 15 minutes as needed, up to 1 mg total. We’ll also give you Phenergan for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I usually don’t take narcotics at home, so I don’t want to get used to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This is just for acute flare-ups like today. We’ll use it short-term and then stop once you’re back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve had a dose of Dilaudid and Phenergan. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as sharp. The nausea’s calmed down too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your labs came back—white count is normal, no signs of infection. Your kidney and liver function are stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a headache earlier. I use butorphanol nasal spray at home, but I didn’t bring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a dose of Fioricet, and the nurse said your headache improved quickly. We can arrange for butorphanol to be sent from home or pharmacy if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be great. It works better for me than anything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been watching you for a few hours. Your pain is more manageable, and you haven’t vomited since admission. We’re going to try a small sip of water to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I haven’t had anything to drink in hours. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept the water down, so we’re advancing to clear liquids. If you do well, we may try soft food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about my G-tube? I really think it’s not working as well since the change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. The team agrees it may not be decompressing effectively. You’re scheduled to follow up with your GI doctor to discuss switching back to a larger tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s been bothering me a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did really well overnight—no vomiting, pain is down, and you tolerated a soft diet. Your repeat labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re going to discharge you today. We’ll restart your TPN at home, and you can resume all your regular medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. Everything stays the same—your gabapentin, clonidine, octreotide, all of it. We’ll send a list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid protocol for future ER visits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s still valid. The ER and your pain team know the plan: up to 1 mg IV Dilaudid over an hour, with Phenergan if needed, then discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’d like to avoid being admitted again if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. This stay was just to get you through a flare-up safely. Your condition is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the fatty liver the CT mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s been seen before and is stable. It’s likely related to your TPN. Your hepatology team monitors that, and no new action is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my iron and thyroid meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue both. Your anemia is chronic, and thyroid levels are stable. Keep taking levothyroxine and ferrous sulfate daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my femoral line? It’s clean, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, site is clean and dry. Keep using the ethanol lock as prescribed after TPN to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. A nurse will go over discharge instructions, and you should follow up with your GI doctor about the G-tube. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you only if you really need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just keep monitoring your symptoms and reach out if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here today because of abdominal pain and some dizziness when standing up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. The pain is my usual, but the dizziness is new. I felt really lightheaded yesterday after standing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. In the ER, your vitals showed a fast heart rate—133—and your blood pressure was 147 over 87. You got IV fluids and some Dilaudid for pain, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 mg total. It helped the pain, but I still felt shaky and like I might pass out when I stood up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your orthostatic vitals. Your blood pressure didn’t drop much, but your heart rate went up from 103 lying down to 120 standing. That’s what we call subjective orthostasis—your symptoms don’t fully match the numbers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not really low blood pressure? But it feels so real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is real to you, and we take that seriously. Dehydration can contribute, and you mentioned you didn’t drink much yesterday and had over eight bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been having looser stools. But no vomiting or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show mild dehydration—BUN is 24, which supports that. But your blood count, kidney function, and urine are otherwise normal. No infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could my meds be causing this? I’ve been anxious lately with the holiday coming up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Both clonidine and Abilify can cause dizziness and a fast heart rate. You recently increased the dose of both, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Abilify was increased a few months ago. I’ve been on 2 mg, but now it’s higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your primary care doctor. Since your symptoms started around the time of the dose increase, we recommend lowering Abilify back to 2 mg daily—the dose you were on before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I tried calling my psych doctor, but they weren’t available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We documented the change and recommend you follow up with them soon. Your abdominal pain is at your usual baseline, so we didn’t change your pain plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I just needed the IV pain meds like I get in the ER every few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We also did a chest X-ray to check for pneumonia since your heart rate is high, but it’s clear. No lung or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re stable. We’ll send you home with instructions to reduce Abilify and follow up with your doctors. Keep monitoring how you feel when standing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my TPN? I need to restart that at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your home TPN as usual. All your other meds stay the same except Abilify.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll call my psych doctor this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll also note that your Free T4 was slightly low—your primary may want to check your thyroid dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had hypothyroidism for years. My dose is usually stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just something to keep an eye on. Otherwise, you’re cleared to go home. A nurse will give you discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your help. The dizziness was really worrying me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s good we found a likely cause. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if symptoms change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’ll follow up as recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having a tough time with nausea and pain since your procedure earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after they fixed my femoral line, I started feeling that familiar migraine and then couldn’t stop vomiting—green, bilious stuff. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your abdominal pain—is it in the same areas as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly the same—left upper quadrant and around my belly button. It’s constant, and I’d say it’s about a 10. It feels just like my past obstruction episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your imaging from today—a KUB shows air-fluid levels and dilated bowel, consistent with a partial small bowel obstruction. No free air, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not worse than last time? But why can’t I keep anything down now when I could before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gut motility has been chronically impaired, and with the adhesions from your past surgeries, even small changes can trigger this. We’re going to keep your G-tube on suction to help decompress your bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s unbearable. I’ve been on Dilaudid in the ED, but even that barely touches it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV Dilaudid in small doses every few hours, just like your ED protocol. We also consulted pain management, but they agree it’s very difficult to control with your allergy history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wish there was something more definitive. I’ve heard about PCA pumps—could that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain service suggested rectal Dilaudid as an outpatient option since PCA isn’t feasible without a willing primary doctor. We’re going to try a 3 mg suppository as needed every 3 hours when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than nothing. But surgery—has anyone talked to Dr. ___? I feel like it’s the only real solution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted general surgery, including your prior surgeon. They feel given your extensive adhesions, another surgery would be too risky and unlikely to help. The risk of volvulus is low because your bowel is so scarred down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s risky… but living like this isn’t living. I’ve been feeling so hopeless lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ve noted your depressive symptoms and will make sure your psychiatrist is looped in. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning are stable—your hemoglobin is a bit low at 9.8, but that’s your baseline. No signs of infection or organ failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver enzymes? I’ve had Hep C for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Slightly elevated AST and alkaline phosphatase, but nothing acute. We’ll keep monitoring, but it’s likely chronic changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G-tube is draining a lot—green, fecal-like fluid. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected. It means we’re decompressing your bowel effectively. You’re draining several hundred cc’s a day, which supports the obstruction picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been talking with your outpatient team—your GI, pain specialist, and primary doctor. They agree your pain is extremely hard to manage, but options are limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did they have any new ideas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not really. They support continuing your current meds and adding the rectal Dilaudid at home. We also discussed long-term care or hospice, but I understand you’re not ready for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m only 50. I want to keep fighting. I know it’s bad, but I’m not giving up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we respect that. You’re a full code, and we’ll continue supporting you at home with TPN, fluids, and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved a bit. We’ve switched from IV Phenergan to liquid form for when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hate shots. Can I start drinking anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your bowel is still sluggish. We’ll keep you on TPN and IV fluids for now. We’re cycling 2.5 liters of saline daily at 150 cc per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube output has decreased slightly—from 800 cc to about 500 cc per day. That’s a small sign of improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s something. My pain is still terrible, though. The IV Dilaudid helps a little, but it fades fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving it every 6 hours in a slow infusion. It’s the safest way to manage it here. At home, the suppository should offer more flexibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a few days. Your labs are stable, and your vitals are normal. You’re still not tolerating food, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to go home. What if I get worse and can’t reach anyone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your weekly ED visits for Dilaudid. And if you vomit more or your pain spikes, come back right away. Your femoral line is stable, so we can give fluids quickly if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve finalized your discharge meds. We’re simplifying a few things—lowering your trazodone and amitriptyline doses to reduce sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. Maybe that’ll help. What about my Abilify? Last time they lowered it for dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on 2 mg now, which is your stable dose. We’re keeping it the same. Your dizziness isn’t an issue this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your hemoglobin dipped to 9.3, but it’s not falling. Your electrolytes are normal, and kidney function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia again. Is it from bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of acute bleeding. It’s likely chronic, from your GI losses and nutritional challenges. We’re continuing your iron and multivitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your discharge for tomorrow. You’ll go home with services to help with your TPN and G-tube care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I guess I have to. Will my pain ever get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t promise that. But we can keep adjusting your comfort. The rectal Dilaudid may give you more control. And we’ll keep talking with your team about new options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. Your exam shows you’re alert, pain is stable, and your G-tube is draining green material but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’ve been feeling it race.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate is in the 80s now—much better than the 120s you usually run. Your EKG was normal, no ischemia. Your mitral valve issue remains stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I don’t need another thing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with TPN set to cycle over 12 hours each day—2200 ml with all your nutrients. And 2.5 liters of saline daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before. I can manage that. And the new suppository—I’ll use it only when the pain is unbearable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. One 3 mg suppository every 3 hours as needed. And liquid Phenergan for nausea. Call your doctor if you’re using them more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep seeing my psychiatrist. I’ve been having dark thoughts, but no plans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for sharing that. Please keep talking to her. You’re not alone, and we care about your mental health too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have weekly labs—CBC, chem-10, albumin. Fax them to your GI doctor. And follow up with Dr. ___ in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also keep your femoral line monitored. No redness or issues now, but let us know if it becomes tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Dr. Lee. I know I’m a tough case, but you’ve been kind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re strong, and we’re here to support you. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in. How are you holding up at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but the suppository helps the pain a bit. G-tube draining about 400 cc. I used Phenergan twice yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s within expected range. Keep up with fluids and TPN. If output increases or you feel worse, come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re officially closing your admission. You were in for about 12 days, and we’re discharging you from our records now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. Take it one day at a time. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing your case. You were admitted today with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been really bad. The pain is constant, mostly in my upper belly and around the belly button. I can’t keep anything down, not even water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your G-tube has been draining a lot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been draining dark green fluid with chunks. It’s been like this before, but it’s worse now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of sclerosing mesenteritis and many surgeries, this sounds like another partial bowel obstruction from adhesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a new problem? But why is it flaring up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to the scar tissue from your past surgeries. These adhesions can cause the bowel to kink or slow down, leading to symptoms like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery isn’t recommended right now. With so many prior operations, the risk is too high. We’ll manage this conservatively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What does conservative mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your stomach decompressed with the G-tube, give you IV fluids, and provide nutrition through TPN since you can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had TPN before. It helps, but I hate the line infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re monitoring your femoral line closely. It looks clean, and we’re being careful with sterile technique.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. The pain is still really bad. Is there anything stronger we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started rectal Dilaudid, which seems to be helping. We’ll keep adjusting until your pain is better controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used that before. It helps, but I worry about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch for constipation or drowsiness. But for now, pain control is a priority.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. We’ve started your TPN today to support your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the TPN going to stay the same when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue daily TPN at home. We’re using a non-standard formula tailored to your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart is still racing. It’s been in the 120s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. It’s likely due to dehydration and pain. Your fluids are being increased, and we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it settles. It makes me dizzy sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on your blood pressure and symptoms. You’re not lightheaded or orthostatic, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do an upper endoscopy today to look at the blockage in your small bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they be able to fix it during the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely. The scope may not even get past the tight area due to adhesions. But it will help us confirm what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s uncomfortable, but I’ll do it if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy is done. The scope couldn’t pass a sharp bend early in the small bowel. It’s likely an adhesion or anastomotic site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing changed. It’s still blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a chronic partial blockage. The bowel beyond is normal, but motility is poor. We’ll continue with current management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a small bowel follow-through with contrast. It showed the blockage is stable. The contrast passed into the distal jejunum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s the same as before. That’s actually good news. It means we’re not dealing with a new twist or complete blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s better with the Dilaudid, but I don’t want to rely on it forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for a compounded version of the rectal Dilaudid so you can continue it at home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your kidney function is good, and your hemoglobin is stable despite being low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m always a bit anemic. Is that from the bowel issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Chronic inflammation and poor absorption play a role. We’ll keep monitoring and supplementing iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid? I take levothyroxine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your thyroid levels are stable. Keep taking the same dose. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your pain is controlled, and you’re stable on TPN and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What changes will I have at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get 3 liters of IV fluids daily—more than before—to prevent dehydration. And you’ll continue the rectal Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as in the hospital. We’ll coordinate with your home care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help at home, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home health will assist with your lines and monitoring. You’re cleared to go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Follow up with your GI and primary doctors soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Keep using the Dilaudid as needed, stay on your fluids, and call if symptoms worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for not pushing surgery. I trust this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you with the safest approach. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with worsening abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been much worse than usual. I only ate half a sandwich, but the pain spiked. I’ve had this before, but my usual suppositories aren’t helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a complex history with sclerosing mesenteritis and many prior surgeries. We’ll manage this carefully. Let’s start with IV fluids and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been more tired than usual. My husband just had a quadruple bypass—so much stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Stress can definitely worsen your symptoms. We’ll monitor you closely and adjust treatment as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your abdominal X-ray shows some air-fluid levels, consistent with your chronic partial bowel obstruction. No free air, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a complete blockage? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It looks like a flare of your usual condition. We’ll continue IV Dilaudid and fluids, and hold off on oral intake for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay with that. I just want the pain under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your hemoglobin is low—8.6, which is below your baseline. And your ferritin is very low at 9.9. This suggests iron deficiency anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia before. I can’t take oral iron—it makes me sick. And my insurance won’t cover the liquid kind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV iron—ferric gluconate—for three days. That should help replenish your stores without the GI side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving with the IV Dilaudid. We’re slowly reducing the dose and will transition you back to your rectal suppositories soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried I’d need stronger meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding anything you’re allergic to. Your pain team reviewed your case and agreed with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back with mixed flora—likely contamination. No infection, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wasn’t feeling feverish, so that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home Lovenox for DVT prevention. You’ve had recurrent clots before, so we’ll keep that up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I can’t tolerate full-dose anticoagulation. This dose has worked before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll stick with what’s safe and effective for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your femoral line—the one for your TPN—has developed a crack. It needs to be replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. That’s the one in my leg, right? Is it safe to replace?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s in your right femoral vein. The procedure is routine. We’ll use imaging guidance to place a new Hickman catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. Just let me know what to expect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was successfully replaced today. It’s now functioning well. The tip is at the cavoatrial junction, which is ideal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt some discomfort during the procedure, but not too bad. Now my thigh aches a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely a superficial nerve irritation from the procedure. It should improve over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. It’s a new kind of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your leg because of the pain. Good news—no DVT. The veins look normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. The pain should settle with time. We’re continuing the ethanol lock for your line care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray confirms the new line is in the right place. There was a small issue—the radiologist initially said the tip was in the atrium, but it’s actually at the junction, which is correct.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard the infusion company had a problem with that. Did it get sorted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the radiologist amended the report. The nurse also spoke with the company so it won’t delay your TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s one less thing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Pain is controlled, anemia is being treated, and your line is working. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your usual meds, TPN, and 3 liters of IV fluids daily. We’re sending you home with extra Dilaudid suppositories for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron? Do I need more after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The three-day IV course should be enough. We’ll check your levels in a week with a CBC and iron panel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on it. If it worsens or you develop swelling, call us. Otherwise, it should resolve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Do not advance your diet without talking to Dr. Lee first. Stick to your G-tube feeds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll wait for instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your condition is stable—pain controlled, labs improving, and line functional.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. It’s been a long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your prescriptions and home instructions. A nurse will follow up with you this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another Lupron shot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one dose is included in your discharge meds. Take it as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood sugar strips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One month supply for monitoring, as usual. Only use if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Call if anything changes. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will be here soon to take you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if I need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will assist you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. You came in with nausea and vomiting, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It’s been going on for about 10 days. Feels just like my past blockages—tightness and pressure all over, especially upper left and right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had similar episodes before with your mesenteric fibromatosis. You mentioned the pain didn’t get better with your usual morphine suppository?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I took it, but the pain stayed strong. I only vomited once this morning, but the nausea is constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve started your TPN through your femoral line, and you’ll stay on IV fluids. We’ll hold off on food for now—NPO—to let your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’ve done this before. But can we do something for the nausea? The IV Phenergan helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV Phenergan now, but we’ll also try a rectal suppository later to see if that works better for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My last bowel movement was this morning—loose and pencil-thin, like always during a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’re still passing gas, just less than usual. That’s consistent with your history. We’ve ordered an abdominal X-ray to check for obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the X-ray won’t show a blockage? Because it feels like one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray came back. It shows a nonspecific bowel gas pattern—no clear sign of obstruction. There’s stool and air in the rectum, but nothing blocked higher up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Huh. So why do I feel this way if there’s no blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain and nausea are likely due to your chronic motility issues and fibromatosis flare. Even without a physical blockage, your gut can act like it’s obstructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, okay. So we treat it like past flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll continue IV fluids, use IV Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, and keep the morphine suppositories. We’ll also add glycerin suppositories to help move things along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The rectal Phenergan seemed stronger than the IV. Can I keep using that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll switch to PR Phenergan as needed. We’re also going to try advancing you to clear liquids later if you’re still doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ve been on TPN for so long, I miss tasting things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. If you tolerate clear liquids, we can gradually build up. But if you start vomiting again, we’ll go back to NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on clear liquids since yesterday. How’s your stomach holding up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pretty good! No vomiting. I’d like to try a soft food—maybe applesauce or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can add those. But let’s hold off on a full regular diet for now. We don’t want to trigger another episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I tried a regular meal last night—just mashed potatoes and chicken—and I threw up twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry to hear that. We’ll switch you back to clear liquids. Your GI doctor agreed—better to go slow. You can start advancing again at home when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. It’s frustrating, but I don’t want to be back here next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a prescription for rectal Phenergan to use at home so you can manage nausea early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Hemoglobin is 10.6, which is better than your baseline. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my femoral line—infusions have been burning a bit the last day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed mild redness. We’re going to do a line study tomorrow to check for a leak or tear. You’ll need contrast, so we’ll pre-treat with prednisone since you’ve had reactions before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I get hives with iodine. So this is just a scan to check the line, not surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s a fluoroscopy. If there’s a small tear, they can often repair it during the same procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling the line study for tomorrow morning. You’ll get 50 mg prednisone tonight and again tomorrow, 3 and 1 hour before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my Lupron injection—is it due soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had your last one about three weeks ago, so yes, we’ll give you your monthly Lupron while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want the fibromatosis to flare more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line study is done. There was a small tear near the hub of the red lumen, but they repaired it successfully. No leak in the tunneled part.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s fixed? No replacement needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. The catheter itself is intact. We’ll continue using it for TPN. You’ll need to do daily ethanol locks to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—2 mL per lumen, not for IV use. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on clear liquids for two days with no vomiting. How’s your pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Pain is mild, maybe a 3. I’ve been using the morphine suppository once a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep your pain meds as is. At discharge, we’re increasing the morphine suppository to 20 mg every 6 hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s higher than before. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s within your usual range. You’ve needed more during flares, and we want you to have enough at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
