conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And I’ll keep using the rectal Phenergan as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 25 mg every 6 hours if nauseated. We’re adding that to your discharge meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your home TPN through the femoral line. Stay on clear liquids for a few days, then slowly add soft foods as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your regular meds continue—Lupron, levothyroxine, gabapentin, and the rest. We’re just adjusting the pain and nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please follow up with Dr. ___ in one week. Call sooner if you have severe pain, vomiting, or redness at the line site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge orders are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—abdomen soft, pain controlled, no nausea. Keep using the ethanol lock daily on your line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll start advancing my diet slowly, like we talked about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call your team if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the X-ray didn’t show a blockage. That was worrying me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s reassuring. Your symptoms were due to your chronic condition, not a new obstruction. That’s why the conservative approach worked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my migraines—they’ve been okay, just baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we treated them as needed with sumatriptan and butorphanol. No new neuro issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried the pain meds might trigger more headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We monitored that closely. You’re on the same regimen as before, so it shouldn’t be an issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hemoglobin—is it okay that it’s 10.6?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for you, that’s actually good—better than your usual 25% hematocrit. No need for iron infusion this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I don’t miss those IV treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on oral ferrous sulfate. Stay consistent with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my constipation—I’ve been using senna and Miralax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep that up. We’re discharging you with both to prevent backup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned—better to stay ahead of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart approach. You know your body best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my asthma. I used my inhaler a couple times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we had albuterol available. Your lungs sounded clear. Just keep using it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I think that’s everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re all set. Discharge paperwork is ready. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with a fever—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took my temperature at home and it was 100.5. I’ve been checking it because the skin around my femoral line looks a little red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chills, sweats, or feeling generally unwell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chills or rigors. I just noticed the redness and thought I should get it checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. We’ll check your blood cultures and look at your line. Your white count is a bit high, which supports checking for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve had line issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. The redness is mild, no pus or swelling, so it may not be a full infection. But with your TPN line, we don’t want to take chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. I’ve also been having pain during infusions through the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned that. We reviewed your recent tube study—it showed no leak in the tunneled part. A small tear in the outer portion was repaired before. This pain could be from irritation or minor inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might not be infected, just irritated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep monitoring. We’ve started IV fluids because your creatinine is a bit high—likely from not keeping fluids down at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I’ve still been nauseous and threw up yesterday. I’m also constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s part of your chronic condition. We’ll keep you on your usual meds—morphine and promethazine—for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The suppositories haven’t been helping much. I think they’re leaking out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll note that. We can adjust the dose or timing. For now, we’ll continue them and use IV Dilaudid if you need breakthrough pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back—it shows mixed flora, likely contamination. So no UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No growth so far, which is reassuring. We’ll keep checking over the next 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 1.2, up from your baseline of 0.8–0.9. But it’s already improving with fluids. Likely due to dehydration from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like temporary, pre-renal kidney injury. As long as we keep you hydrated, it should fully recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been afebrile since yesterday—no fever at all. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. Your white count has dropped from 10.4 to 5.6—another good sign. Blood cultures still show no growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out completely, but it’s unlikely. The mild redness and pain at the line site may just be irritation. We’ll continue the ethanol locks as prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I get another line study?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I spoke with the IV nurse who’s managed your line before. She recommends a follow-up study as an outpatient, but it’s not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll schedule that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just completed your TPN infusion. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as usual. The infusion site still burns a little, but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll document that. It may be worth evaluating the line more closely in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are trending well. Creatinine is down to 0.7, and you’ve had no fever for over 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. We’ll send you home with the same medications and instructions to follow up for the line study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I keep using the ethanol locks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those as prescribed. They help prevent infection. And keep monitoring the site for increased redness or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood cultures are still negative. You’re stable and ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctor about the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if you develop fever, redness, or pain at the site, call your team right away. Otherwise, keep managing your symptoms as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad it wasn’t a serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. You’re being very proactive, which helps. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand to continue all your home medications, including the ethanol locks and TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same doses, same schedule. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—your discharge labs show your hemoglobin is 9.6, which is lower than before but stable for you. No need for transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic for years. As long as it’s not dropping, I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep monitoring it at your regular visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your migraine meds are unchanged. Continue butorphanol and sumatriptan as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve had one small headache, but it passed with the nasal spray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Everything else still feels stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nausea is the same, and I passed gas this morning, so my bowels aren’t completely stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Keep using senna and docusate as needed for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll go home with instructions to follow up with your primary team and the IV nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them today to schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done well this admission. Focus on staying hydrated and monitoring your line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. You came in with worsening abdominal pain and vomiting—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain has been getting worse over the past week. It’s in my upper left and right belly, near my G tube. My usual morphine suppositories aren’t helping at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned vomiting every day for the last few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily for about a week now. Phenergan isn’t touching the nausea. I haven’t slept well because of the pain and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. We’ve reviewed your imaging—an X-ray showed some air-fluid levels, but no sign of a complete blockage. The surgical team doesn’t think you need surgery right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another bowel obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a complete one. It could be a partial slowdown, which fits with your history of sclerosing mesenteritis. We’ll manage your pain and nausea while keeping you on your TPN through your femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G tube output has also gone way up—1200 to 2200 cc a day. It used to be around 300.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s consistent with increased gut activity or irritation. We’ll keep monitoring it. For now, we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—so your gut can rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. But please, I need better pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re starting IV Dilaudid every 4 hours and IV Phenergan every 6 hours. We’ll watch how you respond and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been so frustrated. This pain is constant and nothing’s working like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. It’s a lot to manage. We’ve asked social work to check in with you—they can help with emotional support and coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that. Sometimes the emotional pain feels just as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain now after the first round of IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, maybe down to a 7 from a 10. But it’s still really uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the IV pain meds going and reassess. Your labs are stable—no signs of infection or kidney issues. We’ll continue TPN through your femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my line okay? I’ve had problems with it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it. There’s tenderness near the site, but no infection. However, the external part of the catheter looks worn. We may need to replace it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? It’s split before in the same spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re aware. It’s likely due to movement and positioning. We’ll plan for a replacement when you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re scheduled to replace your G tube. It was already due, and we think it’s a good time to do it while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I’m worried about more pain afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a routine procedure. We’ll use local numbing gel. Most patients tolerate it well. We’ll give extra pain meds just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G tube was replaced successfully. The old one was removed and a new one placed over a guidewire. The site looks clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt some pressure, but not too bad. How’s the output now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still high, but we’ll keep monitoring. We’re starting to transition you back to rectal morphine and Phenergan since you’re tolerating things better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we increase the morphine? 20 mg isn’t cutting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing it to 25 mg every 6 hours as needed. We’ll watch for side effects like drowsiness or slow breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Pain is down, and you’re off IV meds. We’re keeping you on TPN and your new G tube is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’m still anxious about the femoral line. When will it be replaced?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling it for early next week. It’s important to fix it before it fails completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is now at a 3-4 with the 25 mg morphine. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finally something is helping. I’ve even slept a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep you on the current plan. Social work stopped by—they said you had a good talk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helped. I’m still overwhelmed, but I feel heard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge later this week. First, we’ll replace your femoral line tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Will it be done under sedation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get light sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed and won’t feel much. It’s a quick procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. And my other meds will stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. The only change is the morphine dose—now 25 mg PR every 6 hours as needed. Everything else continues as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You just had your femoral line replaced. It went smoothly—you tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t even remember much. Is it secure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, new catheter is in place, cuff positioned correctly. You can use it right away for TPN and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now that the line is fixed and your pain is controlled, we’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your gastroenterologist and pain clinic as scheduled. And please follow up with your psychiatrist—we think that’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve realized how much the emotional side affects my pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Managing both is key. At home, keep using the 25 mg morphine PR as needed, but hold it if you’re drowsy or breathing slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my G tube and line care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—flush the G tube regularly, care for the skin, and do the ethanol lock for the line daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can manage that. Thank you for listening and adjusting my pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We know this is a chronic struggle. We’re here to support you through each flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It means a lot. I’ll keep in touch with my team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It’s good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have all your prescriptions updated, especially the new morphine dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I don’t want to run out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’ll be filled before you leave. And if pain worsens, don’t hesitate to call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay in touch. I’ve learned to speak up when things aren’t working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Keep advocating for yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for respecting that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s how we get the best outcomes—together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel hopeful. That’s a good place to be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Rest up at home and take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for the support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your home health nurse is set up to help with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve already spoken to them. It’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We want you to feel supported at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge order processed. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with all my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, hopefully not in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so too. But we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s comforting to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Always. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing why you came in today. You were feeling dizzy and noticed you hadn’t urinated much in over a day. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I’ve been lightheaded since this morning. And I haven’t had anything to drink since 6:30 AM because I was supposed to see the IV access team about my femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were NPO in case they needed to do a procedure. But your blood pressure was quite low when you arrived—83 over 50. That’s likely why you felt so dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I’ve been struggling to get my home IV fluids because of insurance issues. I haven’t been able to use them for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a key factor. Without those fluids and nothing to eat or drink all day, your body got dehydrated. We’ve already started you on IV fluids, and your pressure is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I didn’t realize it could drop that much. Is it safe now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure is now 122 over 89, which is much better. We’ll keep you on fluids for the next day or so to make sure you’re fully rehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also wanted to mention—the right groin where my catheter is has been really sore. There’s redness and swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that on exam. There’s some tenderness and induration around the tunnel site. We’re concerned it might be irritated or starting to extrude.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been painful for a few days. I was hoping they could fix it when I saw the access team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to re-tunnel the catheter. A radiologist will move it to a new path under the skin to relieve the pressure and pain. It’s a minor procedure, done with imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Will I be awake? I’m a bit nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be given light sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed and won’t feel pain. The team will monitor you the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow afternoon. We want to stabilize your hydration first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain—my morphine suppositories aren’t helping much, even at 25 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you were recently increased from 20 mg. Since you’re not here for an acute pain flare, we won’t adjust your home dose. But we can give you small IV doses of Dilaudid while you’re here for comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. Honestly, if the morphine keeps not working, I might stop it. It feels pointless to keep increasing it if it doesn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely valid. Chronic pain is complex, especially with your history. We’ll make sure your pain management team knows how you’re feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back—no infection. Blood cultures are also negative. So we’re not starting antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be an infection with the redness in my groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The redness is more likely from the catheter tunnel irritation. Since there’s no infection, we can proceed safely with re-tunneling later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my blood work—anything concerning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was low yesterday but has improved. Hemoglobin is stable, and electrolytes are normal. Albumin is 3.8, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. I’ve been worried about being anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re actually doing better than your baseline. Keep taking your ferrous sulfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Today’s the day for your catheter re-tunneling. The radiology team will see you around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little anxious. Is the procedure safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very safe. They’ll use imaging to guide everything. You’ll be sedated, and the catheter tip will be confirmed in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it should help the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, moving it to a new tunnel should relieve the pressure and irritation. It’s been done successfully before in similar cases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. How are you feeling after the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit groggy, but okay. They said it went well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the catheter was successfully re-tunneled. The tip is in the right atrium, and the line is ready to use. The old site is closed and dressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I hope this helps the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it. You can resume your TPN through the line now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been doing well. Your blood pressure is stable, and you’re tolerating fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Less dizzy, and my mouth isn’t dry anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your catheter site looks good, and there are no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my pain meds? My prescription from the pain clinic got lost in the mail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a new script for morphine suppositories—20 mg and 5 mg doses. You’ll have enough to last until your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my other meds—everything stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications continue as before. Gabapentin, levothyroxine, ferrous sulfate, everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been feeling more down lately. All these hospital visits are exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Psychiatry and social work spoke with you, and they agree your depression is worsening. Please keep following up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. It helps just to talk about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’re finalizing your discharge. You’re alert, walking independently, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: low blood pressure was due to dehydration from missed fluids and fasting. Stay on your IV fluids at home if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Insurance is still a problem, but I’ll work on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help connect you with resources. And keep your follow-ups with GI, pain management, and mental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening to me about the pain meds and everything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your care is a team effort. We’ll make sure your records are sent to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much more stable now. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions, and you can head home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having chills and feeling unwell for a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about three days. I’ve had chills, but no fever at home. My stomach pain is the same as usual, but I just feel off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on TPN through a femoral line. Can you tell me how much you’ve been eating by mouth lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking Ensure and eating small meals. Not a lot, but something most days. Why? Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s actually important. We’re concerned your line might be infected. Blood cultures from outside showed Pseudomonas, which is serious. We’ll need to remove the current line and place a new one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I just had one replaced last week after it ‘blew’ during a scan. This is exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But we need to stop the infection. We’ll place a new line in your left femoral vein tomorrow with imaging guidance. You’ll get antibiotics too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I need the TPN. I can’t eat enough to survive without it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your intake closely. Nutrition will assess you. For now, we’re holding TPN to see what you can tolerate by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your abdominal X-ray shows distended bowel loops, consistent with ileus. It’s likely related to your chronic motility issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so bloated? Will it get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping an eye on it. No signs of obstruction. We’ll keep you NPO for now and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We replaced your G-tube today. It had been displaced. You tolerated the procedure well under light sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I didn’t even feel much. Is the old line still in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, until tomorrow when we place the new one. We’re waiting on final blood cultures to confirm the infection source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat blood cultures are negative. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we still need to address the line. We’re proceeding with placement of the new left femoral line tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to place your new line. It’ll go into your left femoral vein with ultrasound and fluoroscopy. You’ll get light sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it stay in long? I’m so tired of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for it to be temporary. We’re also evaluating whether you still need TPN, given you’ve been eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new line is in, tip at the cavoatrial junction. It’s working well. We’ll start antibiotics through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. But I’m confused—why are we questioning TPN now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because insurance requires proof you can’t eat. Nutrition reviewed your intake and thinks you’re taking in enough calories. We’re trying to wean you off TPN safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been more alert today. We held gabapentin and Ativan—they were likely making you sleepy and unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel clearer. But I need Ativan for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart it with meals. You did well on it yesterday. We just needed to rule out sedation as a cause of your confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low vitamin D and calcium. Endocrine is starting you on high-dose vitamin D, calcitriol, and calcium supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on vitamin D before. Why so high now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your level was 20—deficient. We’re correcting it aggressively to help your bones and muscles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry saw you yesterday. They’ll keep you on aripiprazole, trazodone, and lorazepam for anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling hopeless. Hospitalizations keep happening. I don’t know how much longer I can do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. It’s overwhelming. But we’re making progress. You’re fighting a lot, and we’re here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating oral intake well—Ensure, broth, crackers. Nutrition agrees you don’t need TPN anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ll get dehydrated. I’ve always needed IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been watching your labs and urine output. You’re staying hydrated. Your kidneys are fine. You’re doing better than you think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All blood cultures since admission are negative. The Pseudomonas infection is cleared with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We need to remove the line since you don’t need TPN. We’ll finish your antibiotic course first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on oral levofloxacin now. Almost done with the full course for Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the line will come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Once antibiotics are complete, we’ll remove it. It’ll lower your infection risk long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off TPN for days and labs are stable. You’re maintaining nutrition by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still don’t believe it. But I guess I have to trust the numbers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your body is adapting. That’s a win.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to remove the femoral line tomorrow. You’ll finish antibiotics today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Minimal discomfort. Local anesthetic, then gentle pull. We’ll apply pressure after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line is out. No bleeding, no complications. Great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel… lighter. Like a weight is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. You’ve been through a lot. Now we focus on recovery at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating your home meds well—morphine for pain, phenergan for nausea, octreotide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still working on tapering morphine for the transplant eval.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s an important step. We’ll support you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge is coming up. You’ll go home with services—nursing check-ins, follow-up with GI, endocrine, and pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to keep drinking Ensure and watching my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Weekly weights. Call if you lose more than 2 pounds or feel dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look good. WBC is low but stable, calcium improved, no infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really going home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve made great progress. You beat the infection, came off TPN, and your line is out. You should be proud.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re discharged. Keep taking your new meds—high-dose vitamin D, calcium, calcitriol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I have my follow-up with endocrinology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and GI for transplant prep. Call us if you have fever, redness at the old line site, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was scared, but you all helped me believe I could do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard work. We’re just glad to see you healing. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because you've been vomiting and not keeping fluids down. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since I got home last time, I’ve only been able to eat tiny bites. Every time I drink more than a few sips, I throw up—mostly stomach stuff, but once it was greenish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how much are you drinking in a day now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a liter, if I’m lucky. My urine’s dark, and I feel weak. My nurse came by and said I was dehydrated, so she brought me in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your labs show your kidney function is a bit off—creatinine is 1.3, which is high for you. We think it’s from not taking in enough fluids. We’ll start IV fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that fix my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in cases like this, it usually does. Your baseline is 0.7, so we expect it to come back down as you get hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My stomach pain is the same as always, but the nausea is worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on your usual meds—morphine suppository for pain, phenergan for nausea. We’ll also check your G-tube. Sometimes if it shifts, it can cause more nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine output is improving, and your creatinine dropped to 1.1. That’s a good sign the IV fluids are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still feel nauseous. And my G-tube isn’t draining like it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. We’re going to order a quick imaging test to check the position of the tube. It might have moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows your G-tube is still in the stomach, but pointing toward the top. That might not be helping with venting. We’ll monitor, but it might need adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I’m so nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If it’s not in the right spot, it can’t drain well, and that builds up pressure. We’ll see if it shifts on its own first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started tracking your calorie intake. You’re eating about 1,200 calories a day. That’s below what you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try, but I just can’t keep food down. I feel like I’m failing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This isn’t your fault. We’re looking at all possibilities—physical and emotional. We’ve asked psychiatry to talk with you, if that’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been depressed. I even thought about ending it. I made a list of ways… I know it’s not the answer, but I feel so trapped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. That takes courage. We’ll get you support. A sitter will stay with you for safety, and the psych team will meet you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatry team met with you. They agree you’re depressed and having suicidal thoughts, but you’re future-focused—especially on your kids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I wouldn’t do it. But I liked having someone to talk to—the sitter was nice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They noted that too. We’ll stop the sitter, but you’ll have a follow-up with your therapist soon. We also added gabapentin for nerve pain and ranitidine for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube output is still low, and nausea is persistent. We did another scan. The tip has moved into your duodenum—the first part of the small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not in the stomach anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. That explains why you can flush it but not aspirate. We recommend replacing it with a shorter tube so the tip stays in the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Better venting should reduce pressure and vomiting. The procedure is quick and done with imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I agree.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from radiology. The team successfully replaced your G-tube. The new one has a shorter tip and is now positioned in your stomach antrum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it go okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no complications. They used a wire to guide it and confirmed placement with contrast. We’ll start testing drainage soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your new tube is draining well. That should help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your kidney function is back to normal—creatinine is 1.0. Your white count is low at 2.7, but we don’t see infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means you’re more vulnerable to infection, so we’ll watch for fever or chills. But it could also be from your chronic condition or meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I had a line infection. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t either. That’s why we can’t put in a new feeding line without proper care, like an ethanol lock. Insurance doesn’t cover it, and without it, the risk is too high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. But we’re helping you apply for special assistance that might cover it. Someone already sent paperwork to start the process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll finish the application. I just want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all do. You’ve made progress. Pain is better, kidneys are normal, and your G-tube is working. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eat small, frequent meals. Sip fluids slowly. Use your G-tube for venting as needed. Keep taking all your meds, including the new ranitidine and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to stay hydrated. If you can’t keep anything down for 24 hours, or your urine stays dark, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain and nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—morphine suppository every 6 hours as needed, up to 4 times a day. Phenergan suppository for nausea. And your IV Ativan is only for hospital use, so we won’t send that home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PCP, GI doctor, pain specialist, and therapist should all be involved in your care. We’ll send them a summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Dr. ___ is my pain doctor—he knows me well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we consulted him. He agreed to increase your morphine to every 4 hours if needed, but you’ve been doing well with 4 doses a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reminded you to keep up with vitamin D, calcium, and thyroid meds. Those are important long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take them every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. One last thing—your social worker and IV access team are great resources. Include them in future hospitalizations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—the G-tube was removed and replaced this morning, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, around 9:30. It went smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And your pain is still manageable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about a 4 out of 10. Better than last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’ll update your summary and get you discharged soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You’ll go home with a walker for support, and home health will check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I have help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember to follow up with your doctors and keep working on that application. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any new pain, nausea, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vitals are good—heart rate 82, blood pressure 118/74. Lungs clear, abdomen soft. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time. The transport team will bring the wheelchair shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your G-tube site looks clean. Keep the dressing dry and change it every few days unless it gets wet or soiled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done this before. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And call if you see redness, swelling, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, everything’s set. You’re discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this admission. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been vomiting a lot—clear fluid, mostly. My G-tube’s been draining over 1800cc a day. I can’t keep anything down, not even sips of water. And the pain… it’s worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you were just discharged a few days ago. How have you been feeling since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Worse. I thought I’d get better at home, but it’s the same. I’m dizzy, I have headaches, and I’ve lost more weight. I just feel… trapped in this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through this. We’ll get you rehydrated and manage your symptoms. Your labs show your kidney function is a bit off—creatinine is 1.4, which is up from your baseline. That’s from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my kidneys failing again? I was scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is acute and reversible. IV fluids should fix it. We also saw low potassium and a high bicarbonate, which means you’re in metabolic alkalosis—common with vomiting. We’ll correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But the pain is 14 out of 20. Can I get something for that? I need Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you IV Dilaudid. But I also need to ask—earlier in the ED, you mentioned suicidal thoughts. Are you still feeling that way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did. I said if there was a bottle of pills, I’d take it. I’m just so tired of being in pain and not getting better. I asked my kids if they’d be okay if I died… they said no, but they understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. That takes courage. We’re going to keep a sitter with you for safety, and psychiatry will come by tomorrow to talk. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be a burden. But I don’t know how much longer I can do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not a burden. We’re here to help. Let’s focus on getting your fluids and electrolytes balanced, then we’ll tackle the nausea and pain together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better—creatinine is down to 1.1, potassium is normal. The IV fluids are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still feel nauseous. And I coughed a lot last night—felt like I was choking on something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned aspirating during a vomit episode. Your chest X-ray shows a shadow in the left lower lobe. It’s not pneumonia—your white count is normal—but it could be pneumonitis from the aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting levofloxacin for six days. It’s precautionary. Your cough should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my belly’s still distended. Is it blocked again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops and air-fluid levels—consistent with ileus. But no obstruction. Your G-tube is in good position, so we’ll keep using it for venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not mechanical. It’s just not moving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your chronic dysmotility and sclerosing mesenteritis are likely contributing. We’ll keep supporting you while your gut resets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture grew E. coli, but it’s sparse and likely from your normal flora. We’re continuing the levofloxacin since you still have a cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it contagious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this isn’t an infection we’re worried about spreading. It’s more about clearing the inflammation from the aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a midline for IV access. Your central lines are limited due to past clots, so this is safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another femoral line. Last time it got infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is a midline in your arm—much lower risk. We’ll remove it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried to cut my wrist last night with a pin. I was in so much pain and no one answered the call bell. I just wanted it to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry you felt that way. The sitter has been re-started. Psychiatry will see you again this morning. Your safety is our priority.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry evaluated you. They’re continuing your aripiprazole and lamotrigine. The sitter will stay tonight, but if you’re feeling safer tomorrow, we may discontinue it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to hurt myself. But when the pain spikes and I feel ignored, I panic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your pain is managed proactively. And we’ll keep the call bell response quick. You’re doing hard work just by staying here and talking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 1.0, electrolytes normal. You haven’t vomited in two days. We’re switching you to oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’m scared to go home. I’ll just end up back here in three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that fear. But you’ve made real progress. We’re arranging home support. Social work is helping with TPN insurance—they’re reviewing your case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been denied before. What if it happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re appealing with clinical notes. It may take 90 days, but we’ll keep pushing. In the meantime, you’ll continue G-tube venting and small sips as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re medically ready for discharge. Your mental status is clear, you’re ambulating, and labs are good. We’ll send you home with levofloxacin for six days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hemorrhoids? They’re bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have external hemorrhoids. Use Preparation H or sitz baths. Stay on the stool softener and PEG.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel anxious about leaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. But you’ve been cleared by psychiatry—you’re not suicidal now, and you can contract for safety. We’ll follow up closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I need help fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your team or come back to ED. And if you feel unsafe, call 911 or go to the nearest hospital. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll take all your usual meds, plus levofloxacin for six days. Keep using the G-tube as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue morphine PRN, but we’ll work on reducing it outpatient. Focus on small, frequent sips and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m scared, but I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re strong. We’ll get through this together. Discharge is set for noon. Take care, and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping take care of you during this stay. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Honestly, I’m exhausted. I’ve been vomiting nonstop—like a liter or more every day. I feel so weak and dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The team told me you’ve lost about 13 pounds since your last discharge. That’s significant. We’ve started you on IV fluids to help rehydrate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been trying to keep track in my intake/output diary. It’s been negative for over a week. I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your labs, and your kidney function was a bit off when you came in—creatinine was 1.3—but it’s already improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys were bad last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was mild this time, likely from dehydration. With fluids, it’s already coming back to normal. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’m just so tired of being in and out of the hospital for this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’ve been through a lot. We’re continuing your usual nausea meds—promethazine and octreotide—and added IV Phenergan and lorazepam since you said they work better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the IV ones help more. The oral ones don’t stay down long enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep using IV as needed. Your G-tube is still working well for decompression, so that’s helping too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wish I could just get IV fluids at home. I wouldn’t have to keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Dr. Patel mentioned you’re still working on insurance approval for home IV or TPN. You may need to complete some paperwork to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying, but it’s so frustrating. No one seems to follow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have social work check in with you. They might be able to help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better—creatinine is down to 0.9, and your electrolytes are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I only threw up once last night. I think the fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your weight is stable at 155 pounds. That’s a good sign you’re not losing more fluid than you’re taking in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried I’d lost more. My home scale said 143, but I guess it’s not accurate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hospital scales are more reliable. And your albumin is 4.4, which means your nutrition is holding up despite the vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been eating when I can—bacon, eggs, fries. I know it’s not healthy, but it’s what I can keep down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard the nurses mention that. Fatty foods might actually make nausea worse for some people. Have you tried smaller, lighter meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I get so hungry when I’m not vomiting, I just eat whatever I want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I get that. But maybe we could try something like toast, crackers, or broth between meals. It might help reduce nausea long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can try. But I don’t want to feel hungrier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with nutrition to suggest some options. Small, frequent meals might help balance that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? Still around your abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s constant. It’s not sharp, but it’s there. My usual morphine helps, but sometimes I need more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you two doses of IV Dilaudid, and you said it helped. We’ll keep using your home pain plan unless it’s not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. I just hate feeling like this all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Chronic pain is tough. We’ll keep supporting you with meds and comfort measures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed you’ve been saying you feel off-balance. Like your feet aren’t hitting the floor right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It’s scary. I’m afraid I’ll fall, especially at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neuro exam was normal—sensation, strength, coordination are all intact. But physical therapy saw you and thinks a walker could help with stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A walker? I don’t want to seem frail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not about frailty—it’s about safety. You’ll have a visiting nurse come to your home to check for fall risks too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, if it helps me stay safe. I do feel better knowing someone will check the house.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gone two full days without vomiting. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel nauseous, but I’m keeping fluids down. I even ate some soup yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. We’re stopping IV fluids now since you’re maintaining hydration on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a day or two. We want to make sure you’re stable and have support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Last time, I got dehydrated again within days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. That’s why we’re setting up the visiting nurse and encouraging you to follow up with Dr. Patel. We want to catch things early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG showed some changes—slower heart rate, more left axis deviation—but it’s stable compared to before. Nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s always been fast. It’s usually in the 120s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and now it’s down to 78. That’s probably because you’re better hydrated. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I do feel less shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll go home with your usual meds and the visiting nurse visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad to be going home, but I’ll miss having help nearby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re stronger now, and we’re setting up support. Call your husband or PCP if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll try those smaller meals. Maybe it’ll help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in from your clinic visit because of nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve been so sick. The pain in my belly is constant—especially in the upper parts and around my G-tube. I’ve lost 32 pounds since I stopped TPN. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your G-tube isn’t draining much anymore—only about 300 cc a day. That’s less than before. We think it might not be working as well. We’re going to replace it today to help with the venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… will that hurt? I’m already in pain even with my morphine every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you some extra medication to keep you comfortable during the procedure. It’s done with imaging guidance, and we expect it to help reduce your nausea and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube was successfully replaced. We put in a shorter one with extra side holes, and it’s positioned well in your stomach. We hope this improves drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’m still nauseated. And I feel weak. I haven’t eaten in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your labs show low calcium and you’re malnourished. We’re working on getting you back on TPN, but we need insurance approval first. In the meantime, we’re giving IV fluids and supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m still nauseous. The promethazine helps a little, but not enough. Can we try something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adding ondansetron and ativan for nausea. We’re also continuing octreotide, which helps slow gut motility. We’ll monitor how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff, so we don’t think it’s an infection causing the nausea. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But my G-tube output is still low. Is that normal after the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s lower than we’d like. We’re concerned there might be a partial blockage at the stomach outlet. We’re discussing with GI whether we need to switch the tube type again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to change your G-tube again—this time to a Wills-Ogelsby tube. It’s designed to work better if there’s a blockage. We’ll do it early this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? How soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it for tomorrow. We want to make sure your stomach can drain properly so you feel less full and nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new Wills-Ogelsby tube is in. Output has already improved—now over 500 cc/day. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Less bloated. But I’m still tired and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’ve been malnourished. We’ve gotten approval for TPN. We’ll place a central line so you can receive it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of line? I’ve had port-a-caths before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This will be a tunneled femoral line in your left groin. It’s safer for now, given your history of clots and abdominal surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also checking your blood cultures to make sure there’s no infection. We’ll repeat them tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—both blood cultures are negative. No sign of infection in your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When will I start TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow. Once the line is placed, we’ll start slowly. You’ll continue it at home through this catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The femoral line was placed successfully. The tip is in the right spot in your vein. You can start TPN this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes time. You’ll start to gain strength and weight over the next few weeks. We’ll monitor your labs weekly to adjust the formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on dronabinol for nausea, but it makes me so sleepy. Can we stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discontinue it. The ondansetron and ativan seem to be helping, and we don’t want you overly drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My pain is still at my usual level—about 5 out of 10. I’m taking my gabapentin and morphine as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected with your condition. We’ll keep your pain regimen the same. We don’t want to increase sedation, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
