conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your calcium is improving with supplements. Your kidney function is stable, and your hemoglobin is slowly rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been using the walker like last time. I still feel unsteady sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue to encourage mobility. Physical therapy can reassess if needed, but you’re doing well walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re stable, on TPN, and your nausea is better controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home with TPN? How will I manage the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A visiting nurse will help at first. You’ll flush the line every eight hours and do an ethanol lock daily to prevent clots and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the TPN runs at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. From 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. We’ll send supplies and instructions. You’ll also take your usual meds, including octreotide and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your GI doctor and Dr. ___ regularly. And you need a chem-10 blood test every week—same day each week—and fax the results to Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time. I’ll make sure it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll also keep you on calcium, vitamin D, and your other supplements. Your hypothyroidism and Sjogren’s are stable—we’ll continue those meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling down. Not suicidal, but just… sad. Is that part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable. Chronic illness takes a toll. We’re continuing your Abilify, lamotrigine, and lorazepam. Please keep talking to your psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we changed your stomach acid medication back to Aciphex. We used ranitidine in the hospital, but you do better on your home regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I prefer it. Less heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You look well—alert, walking, and your abdomen is less tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more stable. Still weak, but better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. We’re discharging you home with visiting nurse support. They’ll help with TPN and line care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep taking all my meds as listed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Especially the TPN, octreotide, morphine for pain, and your psychiatric meds. Don’t stop anything without calling your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I get nauseous again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the promethazine suppository as needed. If it’s not helping, or if you have fever, redness at the line site, or can’t run TPN, call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help stabilize you. Take care, and keep up with your labs and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just want to feel stronger again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You will. It’ll take time, but you’re on the right path. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I watch for blood clots? I’ve had DVTs before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Watch for leg swelling or pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath. The ethanol lock helps reduce clot risk in the line. Stay as active as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay alert. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll make sure your home team has all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. The nurse will go over all instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse showed me how to do the ethanol lock. I think I’ve got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Consistency is key to keeping the line working and infection-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been very engaged in your care. That makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to stay healthy. This has been hard, but I’m hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. Keep up the good work. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re going home stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready too. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were just admitted after coming in from the ER. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… yeah. I got discharged yesterday, but then I vomited six liters of dark green fluid in just 12 hours. I was scared. I didn’t know what else to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds terrifying. I’m glad you came back. We’re going to take good care of you. You’ve been dealing with gastroparesis and stomach drainage issues for a while, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. My G-tube has never worked right since they changed it. I feel full all the time, nauseous, and nothing drains like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. In the ER, they gave you fluids and some medications for nausea and pain. Your blood pressure dipped a bit, but it’s stabilizing now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still nauseous. And I didn’t vomit in the ER, but I feel like I could any minute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV anti-nausea meds for now. We’re also going to check if your G-tube is working properly. There’s a plan to possibly replace it again if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve had so many changes. The last one didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s frustrating. But we’re thinking of switching to a Wills-Ogelsby tube. It’s designed to vent the stomach better and might help with the nausea and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’ll try anything at this point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We started your TPN last night after getting approval. It should help with nutrition since you can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’ve been so weak. Did the insurance finally come through?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they approved it through the end of the month. We’re also watching your labs. Your hematocrit dropped a bit, but it’s stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been losing weight for months. I’m worried I’ll never gain it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re addressing the malnutrition with TPN and will monitor your intake. It’ll take time, but we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduled to replace your G-tube today. The radiology team will do it with imaging guidance. They’ll switch it to the Wills-Ogelsby tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I’m nervous about the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get mild sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed. It’s a quick procedure, and they’ll monitor your vitals the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as I’m not fully awake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube was successfully replaced. It’s now a 12 French Wills-Ogelsby tube. They used contrast to confirm placement, and it looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think it’ll help? I just want to stop feeling so full and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful. The new tube has better venting. We’ll monitor output and your symptoms over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube output has improved since yesterday. That’s a good sign. Less buildup in the stomach means less nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a little better. Still nauseous, but not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on Phenergan and Ativan for nausea. We tried dronabinol, but you said it made you too drowsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I couldn’t stay awake. I’ve had that problem with other anti-nausea meds before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stick with what’s working and avoid the ones that cause sedation. We’ll also keep monitoring for dehydration and electrolyte issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. No signs of infection. We’re continuing TPN nightly and your G-tube is draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’ve been feeling… really alone. My husband tries, but he doesn’t get it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. This is a lot to handle. Would you like to talk to someone from our mental health team?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe. I’ve had depression for years. It’s worse when I’m sick like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can get you support. You’re not alone in this. We’re here to help with both your physical and emotional health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The mental health team met with you yesterday. They noted dysthymia and some suicidal thoughts. We’re going to keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to hurt myself. I just feel trapped by my body. I can’t eat, I vomit, I’m stuck with tubes…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re working to improve your quality of life. The new tube and TPN are steps forward. We’ll keep adjusting as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray yesterday. It showed no bowel obstruction. The gas pattern is normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had obstructions before. I get scared when I stop passing gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This scan shows things are moving. Your G-tube is helping decompress the stomach, which reduces that risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gone two days without vomiting. Your nausea is milder. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel sick, but not as bad. I can rest more now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also managing your other conditions—asthma, thyroid, and mitral valve issues—all stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a few days. You’ll go home on nightly TPN through your femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have help at home? I’m worried about managing the TPN myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a visiting nurse will come weekly to check your labs and line. You’ll also have follow-up with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chem-10 panel came back normal. No dehydration or electrolyte issues. That’s great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about my kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Everything looks stable. We’re also watching your hepatitis C, but no signs of liver problems now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll take Phenergan and Ativan for breakthrough nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No dronabinol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off due to the drowsiness. If needed, we can try something else later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray today shows continued improvement. No obstruction. Your stomach is decompressing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been scared of another blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home. What if it happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have support. Call your nurse or the PACT team if symptoms worsen. Don’t wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s TPN went smoothly. Your vitals are stable. We’re on track for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready, but I’m still scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay to feel that way. You’ve been through a lot. We’ll make sure you’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge orders are in. You’ll go home with TPN supplies, meds, and a nurse visit scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Just hoping this tube works long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful too. Keep up with your follow-ups, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will come by with your discharge paperwork and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—your husband is on his way to pick you up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’ll be here in about 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll have everything ready for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your visiting nurse will call you tomorrow to confirm her visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I was worried about being on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. We’re all part of your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final reminder—keep an eye on your G-tube site for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And call if it leaks or gets painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same for fever, vomiting, or increased pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your husband just arrived. We’ll get you discharged shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will wheel you out now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with some fevers and a red area near your line. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this morning I noticed a pink spot near my femoral line. It was tender and had some crusting. After dinner, I felt dizzy and my sons saw me shivering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You said your temperature peaked at 99.7°F. Did you take anything for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t take anything. I just kept checking it every 20 minutes. I didn’t want to come to the hospital, but my sons insisted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by getting it checked. We’re concerned about a possible infection at your line site. We’ve started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about losing the line. It’s my only access for TPN. My arms are all scarred over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know how important it is. The line doesn’t look infected along the tunnel, and you’re not running a high fever. We’re going to try to keep it in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been doing dressing changes, but my husband used to do them. I’ve only done it twice myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You explained the steps well. We’ll have a nurse come in the morning to help train your caregiver. We want to make sure it’s done safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures are still pending, but you’re afebrile and the line site looks stable. We’re going to treat the redness with topical bacitracin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe to use with my allergies? I’m allergic to a lot of things—sulfa, Bactrim, even Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bacitracin is safe. It’s not related to the antibiotics you’re allergic to. We’ll apply it only to the small area of redness during dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also felt confused last night, and my vision was blurry. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it might be from the alprazolam you took. It can cause drowsiness and confusion, especially with your other medications. We recommend stopping it for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take it for anxiety. My husband passed away recently, and I’ve been struggling. I don’t want to feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep your other anxiety meds like lorazepam and paroxetine. Please follow up with your psychiatrist to adjust your treatment safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your condition has improved. The redness is still there but not worse. We’ll send you home with instructions to continue the bacitracin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still pending. If they come back positive, your doctor will contact you. For now, we’ll monitor at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I can go home. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your enoxaparin dose adjusted to 30 mg twice daily for better clot prevention. And remember—no alprazolam until you speak with your provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my sons will help with the dressing changes now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. A visiting nurse will also check in to help with the line care and monitor the redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared I’d lose the line or get really sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being very proactive. We’ll make sure you have all the support you need at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be discharged soon. Keep taking your other medications as prescribed, and call if the redness spreads or you develop a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing why you came in. You’ve been having worsening abdominal pain and vomiting for about two weeks, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been terrible. The pain is way worse than usual—like a 9 out of 10. And I’ve been vomiting up to four liters at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned it feels like one of your partial bowel obstructions. That makes sense. We did a CT scan, and it shows your small bowel is still chronically obstructed, just like before—no new changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not worse? But why does it hurt so much more now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be an 'acute on chronic' flare-up—your usual obstruction, but something’s making it act up. You said you’ve been eating—was that since your last visit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I was told not to, but I was so hungry. I had some soup and crackers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might be part of the problem. When you have a partial blockage, food can get stuck and make the pain worse. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But how will I get nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on TPN through your femoral line, which gives you all the nutrients you need. We’ll keep that going and monitor your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G-tube hasn’t been draining well either. I think it’s clogged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. When we flushed it earlier, we found food particles stuck inside. That’s not good. We’ll need to replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? It just got replaced a few months ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s frustrating. But if it’s not working, it can’t help decompress your stomach. We’ll schedule the replacement for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad. I haven’t eaten, like you said, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV Dilaudid for pain and promethazine for nausea. Surgery also looked at your case—they agree it’s not surgical. We’ll keep managing it medically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my femoral line? It’s been leaking a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed the cuff is exposed. That increases infection risk. We’ll replace it at the same time as your G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a lot at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But it’s safer to do both together. The procedure team says it might be tough—there’s a lot of scar tissue from past surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Just checking in. Your G-tube fell out overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It just slipped out! I didn’t pull it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It happens, especially if it’s clogged or not secured well. Don’t worry—we’ll replace it tomorrow with the femoral line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so sad lately. My husband passed two months ago, and his memorial was the day before I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry. That’s a lot to carry. We’ve had psychiatry and social work check in with you. Are you feeling okay emotionally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m coping. I just feel overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep supporting you. Your meds are being continued as before—paroxetine, trazodone, and the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray this morning. No signs of new obstruction. Your colon has air and contrast, and you’re passing gas. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not blocked worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks stable. The pain is likely from the chronic obstruction and ileus—your bowel isn’t moving well. But no emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the procedures yesterday. Both the G-tube and femoral line were successfully replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt groggy afterward. Was that from the sedation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you became very sleepy a few hours after. We were concerned it might be a reaction between your pain meds and sedatives. But your urine tox came back negative, and you’re back to normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was scared. I couldn’t wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It looked serious, but you recovered fully. We’ll be more cautious with sedation in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the new G-tube working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s draining well. We tested it with contrast and saw good flow into the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the femoral line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s in place, but it was tough to insert. There’s a lot of scar tissue and calcification. If the cuff pulls out again, we might need to use a different vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. White count dipped a bit but is recovering. Kidney function is good. We’re confident you can go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I still have some pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s manageable with your regular pain meds—morphine PRN. And since you’re not eating, the G-tube can help prevent buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I won’t eat. I learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep flushing the G-tube regularly. A home nurse will visit to help with care and check the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re doing well—pain is better, you’re alert, and your abdomen is soft. We’re discharging you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad, but I’m nervous about managing everything at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have support. The visiting nurse will help with the G-tube and femoral line. And your TPN will continue as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my Lovenox? I’ve been on 40 mg daily for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It might be higher than needed for prevention. Talk to your hematologist about possibly adjusting the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid and dry eyes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking levothyroxine in the morning, two hours before calcium. And use your pilocarpine and Restasis for dry eyes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if pain worsens, the G-tube stops draining, or you see redness at the line site. Otherwise, follow up with your GI and primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for listening about my husband.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Grief is part of healing too. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—what’s that lump near my scar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw a small 2 cm mass on exam. It’s not new—likely scar tissue or a hernia. Mention it at your next visit for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll bring it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. The discharge papers are ready, and transport is arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in because you’ve been feeling unwell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you for coming. It started this weekend—this strange 'wavy' feeling, like my whole body was off. Not dizzy, not lightheaded, just… unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it reminded you of how you felt before getting septic in the past. That’s a very valid concern, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I’ve been through that before, and I don’t want to miss the early signs again. But my G-tube and femoral line look fine—no redness, no discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, that’s reassuring. The triage temperature of 100.4 was repeated and came back normal at 98.5, so no fever. Your labs, EKG, and urine were all unremarkable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’ve also had these episodes—head shaking, like nodding uncontrollably. I can’t stop it. It’s scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve actually seen one of those episodes earlier. You were fully awake, answering questions, and your vitals stayed stable. That’s very important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was aware the whole time. It’s not like my old pseudoseizures—they were different. But I’m worried… my brother had glioblastoma. Could this be something like that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand that fear. But your recent head CT was normal, and there’s no sign of a tumor. These episodes don’t look like seizures or anything malignant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what could it be? It feels so real when it happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be a benign movement issue—something like a tremor or myoclonus. We’ll set up a follow-up with your neurologist in two weeks to go over it in detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thank you. I just want to make sure it’s not something dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve also checked your abdomen. You have some tenderness, but your G-tube is working fine, and there’s no sign of infection or acute obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about this small lump in my lower right belly. It’s been there a while, but I keep thinking it could be something bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We felt that. It’s about 2 cm, soft, and not tender. Given your history of multiple surgeries, it’s most likely scar tissue. You already have an outpatient biopsy scheduled—good plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. And my femoral line? I’ve had clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Site looks clean, no redness or swelling. You’re on Lovenox 40 mg daily, which you tolerate well. We’ll keep that going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I bruise easily on higher doses, so this is what my doctor and I agreed on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. We’ve continued all your home meds—topiramate for migraines, levothyroxine, gabapentin, and the rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a few migraines lately too. Usually with visual aura. I’ve been using sumatriptan as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that available. Your current symptoms don’t seem to be migraine-related, but we’re managing them as part of your overall care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your blood cultures—both came back with no growth. That’s excellent news—no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. I was really worried about sepsis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We also did orthostatics—your blood pressure stayed stable when you stood up. So not related to low blood pressure or dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the head shaking? Did you see it again last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nurse and I both saw it. You were alert, talking, and vitals were normal. Still no signs of seizure activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad you saw it. I was afraid no one would believe me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you. It’s real, and we’re taking it seriously. But based on what we’ve seen, it’s not dangerous. Your neurologist will help figure out what’s causing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ve been stable, labs are normal, and we’ve ruled out serious causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel better, but I’m still nervous about the head shaking at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But remember, you’re safe. The episodes don’t affect your breathing or consciousness. And your neuro follow-up is already set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my G-tube and line? Should I watch for anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on the sites—redness, swelling, or drainage would be a reason to call. But they looked perfect today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the abdominal distention? The X-ray showed gassy bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s some distention, but no obstruction or free air. Likely related to your chronic motility issues. We’ll keep managing it as before—your TPN and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. Physical therapy saw you this morning and says you’re safe to ambulate independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’ll follow up with my neurologist and get that nodule checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if you have any new symptoms—fever, severe pain, or changes in the shaking—don’t hesitate to call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening and not dismissing my concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You know your body best. We’re here to support you, not ignore you. Take care, and I’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re admitted for left rib pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. This morning, I lifted my bag and suddenly felt sharp pain on my left side. It’s different from my usual belly pain—more on the surface and worse with movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You went to the ED earlier. They did a chest X-ray and it didn’t show any fractures or lung issues. You also declined a CT scan to avoid more radiation, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve had so many scans over the years. I didn’t want another unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The X-ray showed no broken ribs. Given your osteoporosis, we’re considering a muscle strain or minor rib injury. We’ll treat it as musculoskeletal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I’ve been in a lot of pain. I asked for Toradol in the ED—can I get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting Toradol twice a day. We’re also giving you a Lidoderm patch for the rib area. It should help reduce the pain over the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been struggling with anxiety and sleep. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can continue your home dose of trazodone at night. We’re avoiding IV benzodiazepines unless absolutely needed, especially with your complex pain history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the rib pain now? We checked on you overnight and you seemed to be resting more comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better, but my belly pain is worse today. I need IV Dilaudid. I’ve been on a pain contract with my pain doctor, and this is what I take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but we consulted the pain team. IV Dilaudid can slow your gut even more and make your abdominal symptoms worse. It’s not recommended for your type of chronic GI pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it’s what works for me. If I don’t get it, I’ll have to leave. I can’t stay here in this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear how frustrated you are. We’re continuing your home morphine suppository, Toradol, and the Lidoderm patch. We’re also giving ketorolac. These are safer options for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They don’t help like Dilaudid. I want to go home. If you won’t give me what I need, I’d rather leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you feel that way. Medically, you’re stable. Your rib pain is improving, and there’s no sign of infection or fracture. We don’t think IV Dilaudid is safe, but you’re okay to go home if you choose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve prepared your discharge. You’re going home with the Lidoderm patch and your regular medications. We’re increasing your Lovenox dose for blood clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to get out of here. The pain’s still there, but I’ll manage at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Please follow up with your pain doctor and GI specialist. Call us if the rib pain gets worse or you have trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for trying, even if we didn’t agree on everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We care about your comfort and safety. Take care, and I hope you feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. You’re cleared to go home with services. A walker will be provided, and home health will check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I just want to be in my own space.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your GI doctor and pain clinic. They’ll be expecting your call. Please keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these prescriptions for the Lidoderm patch and acetaminophen, though I know you said they don’t help much. Use them if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I mostly just need rest and my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fair. We’re here if you need us. Please reach out if anything changes. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted for rib pain, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I lifted a heavy bag and now my left side hurts badly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your chest X-ray. No fracture, but the area is tender. We’ll treat it as musculoskeletal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I also have terrible abdominal pain. It’s constant and worse lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you have a complex GI history. You're on a pain contract and taking morphine at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s not enough. I need IV Dilaudid. I’ve had it before during admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve consulted pain management. Dilaudid can worsen your bowel motility, which is already very slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need relief. Without it, I can’t function. I’ll leave if I don’t get it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you're in pain, but we can’t give IV Dilaudid. It could cause a bowel blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then I’m leaving. I can’t stay here without proper pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you with your home meds and the Lidoderm patch for your rib. Are you safe to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I’m not okay. I’m going to kill myself when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I need to take that seriously. We’ll get Psychiatry to see you right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry has evaluated you. They’re concerned and want to keep you for observation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be here if I can’t have Dilaudid. I pulled my femoral line. I thought I’d bleed to death.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. There was minimal bleeding, but it’s a serious act. You’re now on a 1:1 sitter for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still in pain. And I need my femoral line replaced. I can’t eat. I need TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been watching. You’ve been seen eating and drinking. Nutrition did a calorie count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t keep food down. I’m nauseous all the time. I need the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The count showed you’re taking in about 68% of calories and 29% of protein. It’s low, but not critical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I can’t live like this. I need the line replaced. And I need IV pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GI doctor reviewed your case. He doesn’t feel the line is needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then I’ll just keep saying I want to die until someone listens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We take your words seriously. That’s why you’re on a sitter and seeing Psychiatry daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an upper GI study with Gastrografin. The contrast reached your cecum in 45 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So? I still can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The study shows no blockage. Your bowel is moving things through, just slowly. It’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need the femoral line. I have no other access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand, but without a medical need, we can’t replace it. We can use oral or rectal meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They don’t work. Only IV works. You’re not helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a few episodes where you arch your back and moan. Neurology thinks they may be pseudoseizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’re not fake. I’ve been evaluated. I have real seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep following with Neurology. But during the episodes, you respond to touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t control them. And I’m still in pain. Why won’t you give me Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it could stop your bowels completely. You’ve had obstructions before. It’s too risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. White count is low but not concerning. Kidney and liver function are okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel awful. And I’m not eating because I’m nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve seen you eat meals. We believe you can maintain nutrition without the femoral line for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You don’t believe me. I need IV meds and my line back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry says your suicidal thoughts have decreased. You haven’t mentioned self-harm today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still in pain. But I guess I won’t say I want to die anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. And your pain seems at baseline. The Lidoderm patch is helping your rib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my belly pain is still there. You’re not fixing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve done all we can safely. No new blockage, no infection. We can’t give IV Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you today. You’re medically stable. Your mental state has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still don’t feel better. But I’ll go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your regular meds. Morphine PR for pain, and we’ve adjusted your Lovenox dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No IV access? No Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. But we’ve spoken with your GI and pain doctors. Follow up with them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. I’ll call them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And please reach out if you feel unsafe. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I won’t do anything. I just want to feel heard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. This is complex, and we’re coordinating with your team. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for not giving up on me, even when I was angry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your safety is our priority. We’ll be here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my doctors. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. You’re strong, and you’ve gotten through a tough time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little more hope today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take it one day at a time. You’re going home with a clear mind and safe plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Rest, stay hydrated, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all anyone can do. We believe in you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ve been having excruciating abdominal pain for the last 10 days. It’s worse than it’s been in months. I need IV Dilaudid — it’s the only thing that works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had chronic pain for a long time, especially with your history of sclerosing mesenteritis and multiple surgeries. Can you describe the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sharp, in my upper belly, and goes down in a V-shape toward my belly button. I’ve also been nauseous and threw up a few times. I had one formed bowel movement in the ER, but it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you were given IV Dilaudid and Phenergan in the ER. We’ll monitor your pain and nausea. We also have a CT from outside that shows a partial small bowel obstruction, likely from scar tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need the same IV pain treatment I’ve had before — Dilaudid every 6 hours for several days, then a taper. Why can’t I get that now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your case with your outpatient pain doctor. Since you’re passing stool and your abdomen is soft, the team feels this isn’t a severe obstruction. We’re concerned about overusing strong narcotics without clear surgical need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I know my body. This pain is real. I’ve been in remission before when I used medical marijuana — but my supply’s been unreliable lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll manage your pain with acetaminophen and low-dose IV Dilaudid for now, as we did last time. We’re also using non-medication support like music therapy to help with comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel better. And I’ve been having those body twitches again — like seizures, but I don’t lose control. They come when I’m stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your records mention those are pseudoseizures — not dangerous, but related to stress. We’ll keep an eye on them. Let’s focus on stabilizing your gut and pain safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your albumin came back normal, which is great — it means you’re well-nourished. You’ve had bowel sounds and no vomiting today. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad. I haven’t slept. I need Ativan IV and Dilaudid. The current dose isn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding off on increasing the Dilaudid after consulting your pain specialist. Your exam is benign — soft belly, no signs of surgical emergency. We’re worried about dependency and side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then I might as well jump out the window. What’s the point if no one will help me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear how frustrated you are. But statements like that require us to get extra support. I’m going to call Psychiatry to help us through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry has seen you and recommended a 1:1 sitter for now. They agree your distress is real, but they’re concerned about safety when pain treatment is limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t mean it literally. I’m just in so much pain. Why won’t anyone believe me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do believe you’re suffering. But we have to balance pain control with safety. You’ve had this pattern before — when narcotics are limited, these thoughts come up. We want to help you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m stressed — new marriage, money problems, only one car for four of us. But that’s nothing new. It’s the pain that’s worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve requested a social work consult to help with system frustrations. For now, we’ll keep managing pain with acetaminophen, promethazine for nausea, and your home meds like gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You had a quiet night. The sitter said you slept a few hours. How are you feeling emotionally today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still angry. But I’m not thinking about hurting myself anymore. I just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Psychiatry will re-evaluate you today. If they agree you’re safe, we can remove the sitter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? It’s still here. Are you sending me home with nothing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. You’ll go home on your regular pain plan — oral meds like acetaminophen, gabapentin, and your sumatriptan for migraines if needed. We’re adding scheduled acetaminophen and PRN promethazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No IV Dilaudid at all? Not even a prescription to use if it flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. Your outpatient team feels it’s safer to avoid it unless absolutely necessary. We’ll follow up with your gastroenterologist and pain doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry cleared you — no current suicidal thoughts. The sitter can be removed. We’re glad you’re feeling safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I didn’t want to hurt myself. I just felt ignored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. That’s why we’re setting up follow-ups — with your PCP, GI, and psychiatrist. Your care team wants to support you long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdomen is soft, bowel sounds are normal, and you’ve tolerated food. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my ankle? I came in with a cast already on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We did an X-ray. There’s an unclear spot on the fibula — could be a fracture. The cast’s still needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need to see ortho when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll need to follow up with orthopedics within the next week to check healing and possibly replace the cast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds — like rabeprazole for my reflux? I haven’t gotten it here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not on our formulary, but it’s on your discharge list. You’ll get it filled at home. Same with your Restasis and Salagen for dry eyes and mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my sons — they help me with meds. My husband knows what’s going on too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve listed your husband as your emergency contact and healthcare proxy. He can help coordinate care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s discharge day. You’re medically stable, your pain is manageable, and psychiatry cleared you. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still upset I didn’t get the IV pain treatment I asked for. But I understand you’re trying to keep me safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s frustrating. But your body is responding well to conservative care. If pain worsens, go to the ER or call your doctor — don’t hesitate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling hopeless again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER or call your psychiatrist immediately. Your safety is the priority. We’re here for you, even after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with GI and ortho. And keep taking my aripiprazole and paroxetine like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your home meds are all on the list. Take acetaminophen regularly, not just when pain flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I wish things had gone differently, but I appreciate you listening at the end.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re going home safe. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted for anemia found during your annual check-up. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for coming by. I’ve been a bit more tired than usual—especially walking up stairs. My migraines have also been worse. But otherwise, I’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood count came back low—hemoglobin at 7.6, which is quite low. We gave you one unit of blood in the ER. You mentioned no bleeding—no dark stools, vomiting blood, or g-tube site issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. My g-tube was clipped off recently because it was leaking, but there’s no active drainage or bleeding. I just feel weak and more fatigued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We did a CT scan of your belly, and it didn’t show any active bleeding. But given your history of GI bleeds and anemia, we’re concerned there might be a slow bleed somewhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before—ulcers, gastritis. But I’m on rabeprazole. Wait, you said I can’t have my usual PPI? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re allergic to omeprazole and pantoprazole, so we gave you Zantac for now. Your husband is bringing your rabeprazole from home, and we’ll restart that soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And for pain and nausea—I use medical marijuana at home with a vaporizer. It helps a lot. But I know hospitals don’t allow it. Can I get IV Dilaudid, Phenergan, and Ativan like in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you those medications for symptom control. Since you can’t use medical marijuana here, we’ll use IV Dilaudid for pain, Phenergan for nausea, and Ativan if you’re anxious. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just need something to keep me stable. The migraines are really flaring up too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your sumatriptan and add Fioricet if needed. We’ll also get a CT of your head to make sure nothing new is going on with the headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT head was normal—no stroke or bleed. The old infarct in your left caudate is stable. We’re still concerned about the anemia, so we’re scheduling an endoscopy tomorrow to look for a source of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that safe with my history? I’ve had so many abdominal surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We’ll do a small bowel endoscopy since your anatomy is complex—part of your ileum and duodenum are gone. The GI team will use special techniques to reach the mid-jejunum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my blood sugar—I get shaky if it drops below 90. I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware. We’ve been giving you D5LR fluids to keep your glucose up. We’ll keep monitoring it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, before your procedure—just to update you. Your hemoglobin went up to 8.8 after the transfusion, which is good. We’re still planning the endoscopy for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready. Any risks I should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low risk of perforation or bleeding, especially given your adhesions. But the team is experienced. If they find a bleed, they can treat it during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your endoscopy is done. The GI team found a small arteriovenous malformation, or AVM, in your mid-jejunum. It was actively oozing. They cauterized it with a gold probe, and it’s no longer bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s where the blood was coming from? I’ve never had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. AVMs can develop over time, especially with chronic bowel issues like yours. It’s fixed now. You also got a dose of IV iron to help rebuild your red blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Will I need more iron later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll check your levels as an outpatient. For now, your PPI—rabeprazole—has been increased to twice daily to protect your GI tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—can I go back to them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continuing. We’re keeping a close eye on your pain and nausea with IV meds until you’re ready for oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs this morning show your hemoglobin is now 9.2—still low but improving. No signs of rebleeding. You’re tolerating food well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been eating regular meals. Abdominal pain is at my usual baseline. Migraines are better with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll switch you to oral pain meds today. You had that episode of stuttering and twitching yesterday—was that part of a migraine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it happens sometimes during bad migraines. Feels like my speech gets stuck and my body twitches. But it goes away. My neurologist says it’s not a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We didn’t see any stroke signs, and the CT confirmed no new issues. We’ll keep treating it as a migraine-related phenomenon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried you’d think it was a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered it, but your history and exam point to migraine. You’re doing well overall. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow up with your PCP and GI doctor. We’ve ordered a CBC in one and two weeks to monitor your hemoglobin. Those results will be faxed to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the iron? Should I take supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your doctor will decide based on your levels. For now, focus on eating iron-rich foods and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my PPI—twice a day now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, rabeprazole 20 mg twice daily. All your other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your hemoglobin is stable, you’re eating well, and there’s no sign of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. So the AVM is fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was cauterized and is no longer bleeding. The anemia was due to that slow bleed. You got blood and IV iron, and your counts are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more IV meds? I’ll go back to my usual routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume all your home medications. For migraines and pain, use your sumatriptan and other oral meds. Avoid NSAIDs—they can cause bleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know—on the allergy list. I use medical marijuana at home. Is that okay with the new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not something we prescribe, but if it helps your nausea and pain without interacting, your doctors may be aware. Just keep them informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And when should I worry and come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have dark stools, vomiting blood, dizziness, chest pain, or a severe headache that doesn’t respond to meds, come to the ER. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you so much. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because of worsening fatigue and abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve been so tired lately. It takes me 10 minutes just to get up. I even fell asleep a few times and thought I passed out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your abdominal pain—how has that been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s gotten sharper the last few days. It’s chronic, but now it’s worse. Marijuana helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also saw in your record you’ve been feeling very stressed and mentioned not wanting to wake up. Can you talk about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… divorce, housing issues. I’m not planning anything, but I just feel overwhelmed. I said I’d be okay if I didn’t wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for sharing that. We’ll get Psychiatry to check in with you. Your safety is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I just need help managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do that. Your blood work shows your hemoglobin is low—8.1, down from 9.5. That’s likely why you’re so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the anemia again? I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, iron deficiency anemia. We’ll give you IV iron to help boost it. No transfusion this time since you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. What about my stomach? I was told I might have a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing a KUB X-ray to check. You’re passing gas and stool, no vomiting, so it’s likely not a full obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your X-ray shows mildly dilated bowel loops, but it’s consistent with your chronic condition—no acute blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery or G-tube? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. You’re moving your bowels, so we’ll manage it conservatively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule a colonoscopy to look for sources of bleeding. Your stool test was positive for blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an EGD recently—nothing was found then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, but that was upper GI. This will check your rectum and small bowel areas we couldn’t see before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is holding at 8.1. You’ve had IV iron, and you say you feel a bit more energy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, maybe a little. Still tired, but not as bad as when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Psychiatry also saw you yesterday and said you’re not expressing suicidal thoughts now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m feeling a bit more hopeful. I have plans to meet my son this weekend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep monitoring, but that’s a positive sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Any change in pain or fatigue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is about the same. Still sharp, but manageable. I’m walking more, so that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your colonoscopy is scheduled for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will they treat anything if they find it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll take biopsies. If there are ulcers or bleeding spots, they may treat them during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The colonoscopy found ulcers in your duodenum and rectum. They were biopsied, but no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they serious? Could they be why my blood is low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the doctor said they don’t look like major bleeders. The biopsies will tell us more—results in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on sucralfate four times a day to help heal the ulcers. And we’re doubling your rabeprazole to twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change in meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To reduce stomach acid and protect the ulcer sites. It helps them heal faster and may prevent future bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Will I need more IV iron?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this admission. Your hemoglobin is stable. But you may need infusions as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your pain is stable, you’re eating well, and your mood is better. We’re thinking about discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What do I need to do after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your GI doctor about the biopsy results. And keep seeing your psychiatrist regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron? Should I ask for more IV treatments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, discuss that with your GI or hematologist. Your levels are stable now, but you may need maintenance therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds—sucralfate and double rabeprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take them as prescribed. Sucralfate coats the ulcers, and the higher PPI dose reduces acid. Both help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for any warning signs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If you see black stools, vomit blood, feel dizzy, or get severe pain, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
