conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’m ready to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a discharge letter with all the details. Keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you—for listening and helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling more hopeful now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot. We’re glad to hear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I stop using marijuana for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t manage that here, but discuss it with your pain specialist. Just be aware it can interact with other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll bring it up. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will give you your prescriptions and discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. Keep building on this progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be your hospitalist during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been vomiting and having diarrhea—up to 15 times a day. And now there’s bright red blood in my stool, just small amounts, but it’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned this started after a recent cautery procedure for ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about two weeks ago. I had bleeding ulcers in the jejunum and colon, and they cauterized them. Since then, I’ve had nausea and muddy stools, but no blood—until a couple days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fevers, dizziness, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. But I’m more tired than usual, and the pain is worse. My medical marijuana isn’t helping like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve checked your labs. Your hemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL, which is low, and it’s been dropping over the past few weeks. That’s likely why you’re feeling fatigued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been dropping? That’s not good. I was already anemic last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your iron and ferritin are very low. We’re concerned about ongoing blood loss. We’ll hold off on transfusion for now and try an IV iron infusion to see if we can stabilize you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but if I keep losing blood, will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But because of rare antibodies in your blood, we have to be careful with matching. We’ll monitor closely and only transfuse if absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It’s always complicated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve also ordered stool tests to rule out infections like C. diff, Salmonella, or parasites, since you have diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been on antibiotics lately, and no one around me is sick. I don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still, we need to check. Your history of sclerosing mesenteritis and multiple surgeries makes your gut more vulnerable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the abdominal pain? Can I get something stronger? Dilaudid helps, but I get sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to balance pain control with safety. You do get quite somnolent with IV Dilaudid, so we’re limiting doses and using alternatives like acetaminophen when we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but the pain is really bad. I’ve been through 23 surgeries—this is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll keep adjusting. For now, let’s focus on finding the source of the bleeding. We’ve scheduled a flexible sigmoidoscopy for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that tell us where the blood is coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will check the lower part of your colon and rectum. If we don’t find anything, we may need a deeper procedure like a double balloon enteroscopy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to stop losing blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back—all negative. No C. diff, no parasites, no bacterial infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection. That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s good. It means we can focus on structural or vascular causes. Your abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops, mostly colonic, but no signs of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time. So it’s probably not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re still waiting for the iron infusion results. Your hemoglobin was 7.4 on admission, and we’re watching for any further drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any update on the pain meds? I’m still hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing with scheduled gabapentin and acetaminophen. We can give small doses of Dilaudid, but we’ll monitor your alertness closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you had the flexible sigmoidoscopy this morning. I have the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did they find the bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rectal ulcers from before have healed. The mucosa looks normal. There were a few small spots of old blood, possibly from rectal prolapse, but no active bleeding source was seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they don’t know where the blood came from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from this test. Since the bleeding was small volume and has slowed, and your hemoglobin stabilized for a bit, we proceeded with an IV iron infusion yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my counts kept dropping, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. After the iron, your hemoglobin continued to fall, so we decided to transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did I do with it? Any reaction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated it well. No signs of transfusion reaction. Your latest hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL, which is an improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So I’m not actively bleeding now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of active bleeding. The GI team thinks the bleed may have been self-limited, possibly from a small vessel or ulcer higher up that we couldn’t see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you tomorrow. You’ll follow up with your GI doctor. They may recommend a capsule endoscopy to look deeper into the small bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? It’s better but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your pain regimen the same—gabapentin, rabeprazole, sucralfate, and as needed loperamide for diarrhea. We’ll avoid increasing opioids due to sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just want to feel more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more update—your labs this morning are stable. Hemoglobin is holding at 9.0. No further transfusion needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Make sure to see your primary doctor soon to check your blood counts again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I see more blood, I’ll come right back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with increasing pain and redness around your surgical site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started two days ago. The area’s getting more tender, and the redness is spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You had the gastrocutaneous fistula closure five days ago, correct? And the wound was dry until now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was healing fine. No drainage. But now it’s warm, swollen, and really sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You don’t have a fever or chills, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been afebrile. Just the local pain and redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Given your history of MRSA, we’re going to start you on vancomycin and get some imaging to make sure the infection isn’t deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see what the CT shows. If it’s just superficial, we may just need to drain it at the bedside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. There’s a small fluid collection, but it’s superficial—no connection to the abdominal cavity. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a bedside incision and drainage to remove the infected fluid. It’s a quick procedure, and you’ll be awake with local anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel some pressure, but we’ll numb the area well. Afterward, we’ll pack the wound so it heals from the inside out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Procedure went smoothly. We drained a small amount of pus and packed the wound. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Is the packing going to be painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might feel a bit uncomfortable, but we’ll manage your pain with IV Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried about the E. coli we saw in the swab. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture showed E. coli and Proteus, both sensitive to the antibiotics we’re using. Vancomycin covers MRSA, but we’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But vancomycin isn’t for E. coli, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're right. We started vancomycin for MRSA coverage. Since the infection is superficial and the organisms are sensitive, we may switch or stop antibiotics soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The microbiology report confirms E. coli and Proteus vulgaris, both sensitive to several antibiotics. We’ll continue monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay on antibiotics long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Since the infection is localized and improving, we’ll stop antibiotics once the wound looks clean. Healing will be by secondary intention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? On a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 4 now. Much better since the drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll switch you to oral pain meds soon. Also, your labs show mild anemia—Hgb 7.5—but stable, so no transfusion needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been chronic for years. I’m used to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows anemia of chronic disease. We’ll manage it outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is looking much better—less redness and swelling. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need help with the dressing at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A visiting nurse will assist initially, but you said you’re comfortable changing it yourself. We’ll teach you the steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the packing—how long will that continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until the wound heals from the bottom up—could take weeks. You’ll taper packing as it fills in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for that mean I need to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever over 101, increasing redness or pain, foul-smelling drainage, or if the wound opens widely. Also, no bowel movement in 48 hours—given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—can I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your pre-admission meds except painkillers you’re allergic to. We’ve added rabeprazole for reflux and acetaminophen for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I don’t need more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the wound improvement and superficial nature, we’re stopping antibiotics. The body can handle the rest with proper wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Follow up with your surgeon in one week. Call sooner if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep up with the wound care. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll avoid driving until I’m off pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Safety first. See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re in the ICU right now because you were confused when you came in. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I don’t really remember much. My husband said I was acting strange for two days. I missed my magnesium and potassium pills. Is that why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. We’re also seeing signs of infection and your liver tests are off. Your ammonia level was high, which can cause confusion. We started you on lactulose and antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so sick lately. I had an endoscopy recently for vomiting, but they didn’t find anything. I didn’t have fever or pain then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Right now, your body is under stress—low potassium, infection, and fluid loss from your stomach tube. We’re giving you fluids and watching your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube is awful. It drained so much. Why did I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bowel wasn’t moving—called ileus. The tube helps relieve pressure and lets your gut rest. We’ll remove it once things improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your X-ray shows your colon is still dilated, but no blockage. We’re keeping you on bowel rest for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I ever eat again? I’m so tired and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you anti-nausea meds. Once your bowel starts moving, we’ll try small sips. It may take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg ultrasound was clear—no clots. But your neck and arm veins show narrowing from past lines. That makes access hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many lines. They always say my veins are bad. Is that why I got sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The femoral line placed at the other hospital may have introduced bacteria. We’re treating it as sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are back. You have three bacteria: Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and Staph. We’ve narrowed your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three? Is that bad? Where did they come from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but treatable. Likely from the femoral line. We’ve removed it and are now on targeted antibiotics—vancomycin and ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my confusion? Is it from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s multifactorial—dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and possibly the infection. Your ammonia is down, and you’re more alert. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT neck shows chronic vein changes from past lines. No acute clot, but explains your swelling. We’ll avoid femoral access in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m swollen everywhere. Is that from the fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we gave a lot of IV fluids to treat sepsis. You’ve gained weight, but it’s temporary. We’ll monitor your legs and you can track your weight at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat X-ray shows your colon is still dilated, but stable. We’re starting loperamide for diarrhea that started after the ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought the ileus was getting better. Why diarrhea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes after a bowel slowdown, it rebounds. Your C. diff test was negative, so we think it’s from gut imbalance. Loperamide should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was very high—up to 4. We gave vitamin K. It’s improving. Hepatology thinks it’s from poor nutrition, not liver failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take rivaroxaban for clots. Is that why my blood didn’t clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, but your liver wasn’t making clotting factors well. Vitamin K helped, and we’ve continued your rivaroxaban safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need a new IV line. Your femoral line is out, and your upper veins are narrowed. We’re planning a midline in your arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please be careful. I’ve had so many failed lines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your midline was placed successfully in your right arm. It’s working well for antibiotics and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some atelectasis—lung collapse from shallow breathing. We’ll have you use the incentive spirometer often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been too weak to breathe deeply. Will it get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as you feel stronger. It’s not pneumonia, so no extra antibiotics. Just keep using the device and coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving—INR normal, liver tests better, and white count stable. Your bowel is moving again. We’ll start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! Can I have broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll advance slowly. If you tolerate it, you can move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Your last X-ray shows big improvement in your colon. We’ll remove the NG tube today if you’re still tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please take it out. I hate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We will. Also, your antibiotics are switching to oral—linezolid and cipro—for one more week at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have to take those? Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to finish treating the infection. Linezolid can affect other meds—don’t take your migraine injections until it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are nearly normal. Potassium is stable, bicarbonate at 21. We’ll stop the oral bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my confusion? Could low blood sugar be causing it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t see low sugar here, but we’ll give you a glucometer to check at home, just in case. Your mental status has cleared, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s from the fluids we gave. We didn’t start a diuretic, but keep weighing yourself. Call if you don’t lose weight in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final X-ray shows your bowel is much better. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if you keep doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish your antibiotics, take your potassium twice daily now, monitor your weight, and check your blood sugar if you feel off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them—rivaroxaban, gabapentin, aripiprazole, lamotrigine, PPI, and the rest. We’re sending a list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor and primary care. Labs next week to check electrolytes and blood count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your midline will be removed before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: finish antibiotics, monitor weight and blood sugar, and call if you’re not improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no femoral lines ever again, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’ll note your difficult access. Use your arm veins when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming: you understand your meds, warning signs, and follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—antibiotics for four more days, potassium twice daily, weigh daily, check sugar if confused, and see my doctors next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Midline is out, no bleeding. You’re ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you to check in. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let the nurse know when you’re ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having severe abdominal pain since last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's sharp and in my upper belly, left of center. It gets worse when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you haven't passed gas or had a bowel movement since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing. That’s really unusual for me. I usually have many loose stools every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of sclerosing mesenteritis and multiple bowel obstructions, this could be another partial blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels just like my past obstructions. Is that what the X-ray showed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels, which suggests ileus or partial obstruction. But stool is still moving into your rectum, so it’s not a complete blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now. We’ll insert a nasogastric tube to decompress your stomach and bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s uncomfortable, but I know it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also start IV fluids and give you pain and nausea meds. Your labs show low calcium and magnesium, so we’ll replace those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’m just glad it’s not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your NG tube drained about 460 mL yesterday, and you had three bowel movements. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Is the blockage clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like it. We’ll try clamping the NG tube today to see if you can tolerate it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start drinking water if it goes well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with a clear liquid diet if you don’t have nausea or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed the clamp trial. We’re removing the NG tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. I hated that tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on clear liquids and will advance to full liquids, then soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my IV? It’s been hard to keep it in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled a PICC line placement today for better access, since you’ve had trouble in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Is it done with ultrasound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and fluoroscopy to guide it. It’ll go into your right arm and end in a large vein near your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully in your right axillary vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my arm is burning—sharp pain from shoulder to hand. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted neurology. They think it’s nerve irritation from the line placement, not damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away? Shouldn’t they pull the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They don’t think removing it will help. It should improve with time. We’ll start a lidocaine patch and increase your gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust them. Just want the pain to ease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also advancing you to a regular diet today. You’ve been stooling regularly, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate toast and applesauce earlier—no nausea. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. Your labs are stable—hemoglobin is 9.0, and electrolytes are normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still low hemoglobin, but I’ve always been anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic anemia from your bowel issues. We’re not concerned as long as it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain is controlled, you’re eating regular food, and your arm pain is improving with the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been walking the halls too. Feeling stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual meds. We’re increasing gabapentin to 1200 mg twice daily for your arm nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lidocaine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one patch daily on your right arm as needed. We’re also switching from pantoprazole to famotidine for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my liver history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, and famotidine is safer long-term. You’ll keep taking rivaroxaban for your DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know—no NSAIDs, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stick to acetaminophen or your prescribed oxycodone for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your bowel function has returned, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have increasing pain, vomiting, or can’t pass stool or gas. Also, monitor your arm for worsening pain or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with Dr. ___ as planned. Take care, and we’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and nausea again. Can you tell me what’s been going on since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since I got home, I’ve had constant nausea, barely eating, and lost about 10 pounds. I wasn’t passing gas or having bowel movements, and the pain got worse. I went to the ER and they said it was another blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And they placed a nasogastric tube for decompression. We’ll keep that in for now to help rest your bowel. You’re on IV fluids and TPN for nutrition, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I ever be able to eat again? I’m so tired of not being able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping to find a long-term solution. Right now, your bowel isn’t moving properly due to your sclerosing mesenteritis and past surgeries. We’ll focus on managing this without surgery, since that’s not likely to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show mild anemia and your liver enzymes are a bit elevated, but stable. We’re continuing your TPN through the femoral line for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the TPN helping? I still feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s supporting your nutrition, but it takes time. We’re increasing the volume to help with hydration too. We’ll monitor your response over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a small bowel follow-through with contrast. The dye moves slowly through the upper jejunum but eventually reaches the colon. There’s no clear blockage point, which suggests a functional obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a physical blockage? What does that mean for treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s more about the bowel not moving properly. Surgery isn’t recommended given your history. We’re considering a G-tube for long-term decompression so you can manage symptoms at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A feeding tube again? I had one before, but it was removed. Will this help with the bloating and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this one will be used mainly to vent the stomach and reduce pressure. You’ll also get water flushes through it to stay hydrated. It’s meant to improve your comfort and prevent repeated hospitalizations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled a push enteroscopy to look directly at the jejunum. It may help us see if there are any areas we can treat, though we don’t expect to find a stricture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? And what happens if they don’t find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so it won’t be painful. If no treatable narrowing is found, we’ll proceed with the G-tube plan. That’s still the best option for long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enteroscopy showed dilated jejunum with some sharp turns, but no areas narrow enough to dilate. No intervention was done. We’re moving forward with G-tube placement tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m nervous, but I trust you. Will I be able to go home soon after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait 24 hours before using the tube. Once you’re stable and we confirm it’s working, we’ll start planning your discharge with home TPN and care instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube was placed successfully. It’s not to be used for 24 hours. We’ll start with water flushes and venting after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little sore, but okay. When can I start sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll allow small sips of clear liquids every 8 hours once we start using the tube. You’ll need to watch for increased bloating or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The G-tube is draining bilious fluid, which is expected. We’ve started 150cc water flushes every 8 hours through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I passed a little gas yesterday. Is that a good sign?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a positive sign of some return of bowel function, even if slow. We’re not expecting full recovery, but every bit helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m having trouble finding the right words. And my right arm feels weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order a CT head right away to make sure there’s no new stroke. You have a history of stroke, so we need to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows no new bleeding or stroke. It’s consistent with your old left caudate infarct. We’ll get neurology to evaluate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a new stroke? But why am I having trouble speaking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to your prior brain injury. Neurology will help determine if it’s a new issue or part of your baseline. They may recommend an EEG.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology saw you. They recommend an EEG and a CTA of the head and neck to check your blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another IV? My veins are so hard to access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll place a midline in your arm to give the contrast for the CTA. It’s less invasive than a PICC and should work for this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The midline was placed successfully. The CTA is scheduled for later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. The CTA shows no new blockages in your brain vessels. Your carotids are normal. The speech issues are likely related to your old stroke. Neurology recommends follow-up with your neurologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not another stroke. My arm feels better already. The word-finding is still hard, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll continue to monitor. The midline will be removed before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your TPN volume to help with hydration. You’re also doing well with the water flushes through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my pain meds by mouth now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you’ll need to clamp the G-tube for an hour after. We’re switching you to Dilaudid suppositories for severe pain—they worked well and avoid stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin has dropped a bit, but it’s expected with your chronic anemia. We’re not transfusing—you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m always tired. Is there anything else we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re optimizing your nutrition and hydration. The anemia is chronic, tied to your other conditions. We’ll monitor it with weekly labs at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making progress. You’re tolerating sips, the G-tube is working, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get TPN nightly, 150cc water flushes every 8 hours through the G-tube, and take meds as prescribed. Limit clear liquids to a few sips every 8 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood thinner? I was on Xarelto.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to Lovenox injections twice daily. Because of your bowel issues, we’re concerned you might not absorb oral meds well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to give myself shots? I’m nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will teach you and your husband how. It’s a small needle, under the skin. You’ll get pre-filled syringes. You’ll do fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. You have an appointment with your new GI surgeon in a few days to coordinate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they help me find a primary doctor and neurologist too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll help coordinate all your specialists. You’ll also follow up with pain management for your Dilaudid prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if my belly swells up or I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER if you have increasing pain, distension, or can’t keep liquids down. Those could be signs the obstruction is worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pharmacy will fill your Dilaudid suppositories tonight. Bring both prescriptions—one for 12 and one for 60.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the G-tube care—any special instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the site clean and dry. Rotate the tube daily. Call if there’s redness, swelling, or leakage around it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. We’ll send all your records to your new team. Take care, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’m ready to go home and start feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. We’re confident this plan will help you manage your symptoms. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take it one day at a time. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Travel safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your new team to ensure a smooth transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I appreciate all the coordination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important you have support. Don’t hesitate to reach out if you have questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Wishing you a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. See you soon in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here because of abdominal pain and not passing gas. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain started about 12 hours ago. It feels like my old blockages. I haven’t passed flatus since this morning. I’ve been having these episodes for years because of my sclerosing mesenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned forgetfulness yesterday—has that improved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s gone now. It scared me, but it only lasted a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. We reviewed your CT scans from earlier today. There’s no sign of a complete bowel obstruction, but your G-tube appears blocked. We’ll place an NG tube temporarily to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? I’ve had NG tubes before—they’re uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be uncomfortable, but we’ll guide it gently through your nose. We’ll also give you something to help with the discomfort. It’s temporary—just until we fix the G-tube issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about my G-tube? It’s been acting up since I stopped venting it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely why it’s clogged. Thick mucus built up. We’ll clean it out and may need to replace and upsize it so it doesn’t happen again. That’s planned for later in the week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many surgeries… I just want this managed without another big operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not planning surgery. This is a minor procedure with radiology. You’ll be sedated, and they’ll replace the tube using imaging to guide it. Very low risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? The NG tube is working—your stomach is decompressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is a bit better, but I hate this tube. When can we remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your G-tube is replaced and working well. We’re scheduling that for Thursday. In the meantime, we’re keeping you NPO—no food or drink by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No food? How will I get nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids and electrolytes. Since you’re off TPN now, we’re not restarting it unless needed. Your body just needs a rest right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds? I take gabapentin, lamotrigine, and aripiprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted those. You’re getting them through the IV or crushed, since you can’t swallow pills right now. We’re monitoring for any side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your white count is normal, no sign of infection. But your hemoglobin is low—9.2—and your bicarbonate is a bit low, suggesting mild metabolic acidosis. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve always been anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s consistent with your history of chronic disease. We’re not transfusing—you’re stable. But we’ll make sure you’re getting enough iron and nutrients when you start eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? Still managing okay with the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain is much better. I don’t need it as often. Can I try sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to wait until after your G-tube is replaced. We don’t want to risk worsening the obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just miss normal routines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your G-tube replacement is scheduled for tomorrow morning. The radiology team will upsize it to reduce future clogs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little nervous. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation—fentanyl and midazolam—so you’ll be relaxed and won’t feel pain. Someone will monitor your vitals the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. And after? When can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with a liquid diet the next day if all goes well. We’ll also begin a new medication called methylnaltrexone to help with bowel motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps stimulate your bowels without affecting pain control. It’s especially useful for people on narcotics who have slow motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you just came back from the procedure. It went perfectly. Your G-tube was upsized to 16 French and is working well. You tolerated sedation without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy, but okay. Is the old tube gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, replaced and confirmed in the right spot with imaging. We’ll remove the NG tube later today once we see the G-tube is venting properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube is draining well. We’ve removed the NG tube. You can start small sips of water now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you! That’s a relief. Can I have broth tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you tolerate water, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow. We’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We got your urine culture back—it shows Klebsiella pneumoniae, but you’re not running a fever or having symptoms. We don’t think you need antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a UTI? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but since you’re not symptomatic, we’ll just monitor. Treating it without symptoms could lead to resistance. We’ll check again if you develop fever or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on full liquids and your bowels are moving. We’re going to switch your pain meds to Dilaudid suppositories as needed. You said you have some at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have a few left. I’ll use them sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also sending you home on methylnaltrexone to keep your motility improved. And ranitidine for reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another follow-up with GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in two weeks with Dr. Evans. They’ll assess your G-tube care and overall bowel function. We want to prevent future blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re tolerating food, pain is minimal, and your G-tube is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have severe pain, can’t pass gas, or develop a fever over 101. Also, make sure to vent your G-tube regularly to avoid mucus buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your home meds: gabapentin, lamotrigine, aripiprazole, and the new ones—ranitidine and methylnaltrexone. We’re not giving a new Dilaudid script since you have suppositories at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not until you’re off pain meds. Even then, go slow. You might feel weak or tired for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The physical therapist saw you today. You’re strong enough to go home with visiting nursing services to help with G-tube care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about managing alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge orders are ready. You’re going home today. We’ll review everything with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: vent your G-tube daily, take your meds, and follow up in two weeks. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson—no skipping G-tube care!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s the best way to avoid another hospital stay. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge paperwork and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine culture showed Klebsiella, but since you’re not symptomatic, no treatment is needed. Just monitor for burning or urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if you have migraines or asthma flares, use your usual rescue meds. You’re cleared for light activity, but avoid heavy lifting for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it easy. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when they are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were brought in last night with a fever. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit better. My fever went down after I got here, but I still have this dull headache in my forehead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it’s different from your usual migraines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my migraines are usually on one side and I get that flashing light before. This is just pressure, no aura.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And your nausea—is that worse than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, same as always. My stomach pain is also at baseline. But I’m worried—why did I spike a fever during my iron infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we’re looking into. We’ve done some tests. Your chest X-ray was clear—no pneumonia. The CT of your abdomen showed your bowel looks stable, no new blockages or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. But what about the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood cultures to check for infection. We’ll know more in a day or two. For now, we’re watching you closely and giving your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve had so many lines over the years—I hope it’s not another infection from the femoral catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re definitely considering that. Your line site looks clean, but sometimes infections can come from inside the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have an update—your first blood cultures didn’t grow anything, but we’re still waiting on others. Your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Any idea when we’ll know more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. We’re keeping a close eye. In the meantime, you’re still afebrile, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we just got news—your latest blood culture grew coagulase-negative staph. It’s likely coming from your central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we’re catching it early. We’re starting you on IV vancomycin to treat it. Infectious disease is also involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I need a new line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re trying to keep your current one for now, since access is difficult. But we’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your echocardiogram was limited, but we didn’t see any sign of heart valve infection, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How’s the antibiotic working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been fever-free, and your white count is stable. That suggests it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The nurse mentioned your line tubing looks cracked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I noticed a small split yesterday. I clamped it right away. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It increases infection risk. The team repaired it at the bedside yesterday, but we’ll need to watch for leaks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m back. We just got the radiology report—the repair held, and the line is still functional.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. But if it leaks again, we may need to replace it completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m concerned—the line is leaking again at the repair site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Does that mean surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. Interventional radiology can replace it using a wire guide, so it’s less invasive. We’ll do it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just before your procedure—we’ll use your existing line to guide the new one, so we don’t lose access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—fentanyl and midazolam—so you’ll be relaxed but may remember parts of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, great news—the line was successfully replaced. The old one was removed over a wire, and the new one is in place in your femoral vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the infection under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve been on vancomycin for five days, and you’re still fever-free. You’ll finish a 14-day course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I get the IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Through your new line. A nurse will come to your home to give them twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron I needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now that your line is stable, we gave you the iron infusion today. You tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual ones—gabapentin, aripiprazole, lamotrigine, ranitidine, and Lovenox for clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And pain control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can keep using Dilaudid as needed. We’ll send extra with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m here to talk about discharge. You’re doing well—afebrile, eating, and ambulating. We plan to send you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Signs of infection—fever, redness or drainage at the line site, chills. Also, if you develop abdominal pain or can’t pass gas, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get it IV twice a day for five more days. Also, you’ll use vancomycin-heparin locks in the line when it’s not in use to prevent reinfection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will show me how?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a home health nurse will visit to administer the first dose and teach you and your caregiver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor in a week. They’ll check your line and review your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my G-tube and stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT showed no changes. Keep using the G-tube for venting as usual, and take your nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my migraines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The headache you had was likely from the fever. Your usual meds should handle migraines as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’ll have your discharge papers and meds ready soon. Rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home with nursing support. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with a bad headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started suddenly with flashing lights, just like my usual migraines. I took my sumatriptan but it didn’t help at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it’s similar to your past migraines, which are usually on the right side. This one is on the left now—is that correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s unusual. But the throbbing, the light sensitivity—it feels like the same type. Just on the opposite side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We checked your labs and a chest X-ray, which were normal. No fever or signs of infection. We gave you some medications in the ER—Toradol, Reglan, and Dilaudid. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurting. The pain’s a little less intense, but it’s not going away like it usually does.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of stroke and migraines, we want to be cautious. We’re going to do a CT scan of your head to make sure there’s nothing new going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a CTA recently—no aneurysms were found. But I understand if you need to double-check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was outpatient. This is a non-contrast CT to rule out bleeding or stroke. We’ll get you scheduled right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I have your CT head results. Good news—it shows no bleeding, no stroke, no new issues. Just some chronic changes from your past stroke, which are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why isn’t the migraine responding like it used to?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes migraines can become resistant, especially if they’re frequent. You mentioned your Botox injections help—when was your last one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few months ago. My next appointment isn’t until next week. I was hoping to get it sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your specialist knows you’re still struggling. In the meantime, we’re watching for any neurological changes. You mentioned earlier you had some trouble speaking and weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, last night—sudden aphasia and left arm weakness. But it went away by the time I got to CT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed it. Given the transient nature and your history, they believe it’s part of your complex migraine, not a new stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had those episodes before, always with bad migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. Also, your abdominal pain—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nausea and cramping. No bowel movement or gas in over a day. I have a history of bowel obstructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a KUB—abdominal X-ray. It shows some dilated bowel loops. This suggests ileus, which is a temporary lack of movement in the intestines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a blockage? I’ve had several small bowel obstructions before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray doesn’t show a complete blockage. It’s more consistent with ileus, which can happen after stress or illness. We’ve kept you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now and started IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My G-tube is supposed to help with decompression. Is it working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is in place and functioning. We’re using it as needed. We’ll start you on clear liquids tomorrow if your symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the headache today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as intense. The light sensitivity is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. And your belly—any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still crampy, but I passed some gas last night. That’s a good sign, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’ll try advancing your diet to clear liquids today. If you tolerate that, we can move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And what about the headache? Will it keep improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It seems to be resolving on its own. Since it’s not responding to usual meds, we’re relying on time and rest. Your Botox appointment is key for prevention moving forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re looking more comfortable. Headache still present?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a dull ache now. I didn’t need any pain meds overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. And your abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had a small bowel movement this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Means your ileus is resolving. We’ll keep you on soft diet and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. One thing—my G-tube stitching came loose yesterday. The nurse said it was replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was re-secured. The site has mild redness, but no signs of infection. Keep it clean and dry at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. How are you feeling overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. Headache is almost gone. Belly feels normal. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Your labs are stable. Blood cultures were negative—no infection. We’ll send a summary to your PCP and neurologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get my iron infusion? I missed one while I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled for next week. We’ll coordinate with your infusion center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Botox appointment—is it still on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ve flagged that you’re still having migraines. They may move it up or adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been relying on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We also checked your thyroid—TSH is a bit high, but your free T4 is normal. Your endocrinologist should follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have hypothyroidism. I take levothyroxine—should I adjust the dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not without checking with your doctor. We’ll note it for your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the headache returns severely, or you have weakness, trouble speaking, or belly pain with vomiting, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continued. Take the sumatriptan only as needed, and avoid overuse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your specialists have all the details. Take care, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you hopefully not too soon!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hopefully not! But we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my G-tube site is a little red. Should I use any cream?
